utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone in and around this courtroom, those who are assisting us. Madam Registrar, may I ask you to call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-02-59-S, the Prosecutor versus Darko Mrdja.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Mrdja, can you hear me in a language you understand? Is the translation properly functioning? That's exactly what I -- is the translation now properly functioning?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour, but I can only hear what is being said in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I think we should change the channel for you. Is the translation now properly functioning, Mr. Mrdja?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Everything is fine now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I have the appearances, first for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours. Alan Tieger and Tim Resch appear on behalf of the Prosecution, with case manager Skye Winner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. And for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. For Defence, Vojislav Dimitrijevic, lead defence, and my learned colleague, Otmar Wachenheim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Dimitrijevic. This afternoon this Chamber will have a sentencing hearing in the case of Mr. Mrdja, who has pleaded guilty on an indictment on which only two counts still appear, that is, Count 2, murder, a violation of the laws or customs of war, and Count 3, inhumane acts, a crime against humanity. The indictment, the latest version, the amended version, the final version bears the date of the 4th of August. The Chamber has received the pre-sentencing briefs, both of the Defence and of the Prosecution. The Chamber further has received annexes to both these sentencing briefs, and the Chamber also has received a psychological report that arrived almost immediately after we had received the sentencing briefs, that is, a report made by -- made by Professor Adolf Gallwitz. The order will be that I'll first give an opportunity to both parties to briefly introduce what they want to submit to the Chamber in addition to what has been already submitted in writing, so to set out their argument briefly. Then the Chamber will listen to evidence adduced by the parties, whether it's viva voce evidence or whether it's commented evidence in writing under 92 bis or under Rule 100. As the parties may be aware, the -- the formal Rules of Evidence do not similarly apply as they do during trial. Then as far as I understand, Mr. Mrdja himself would like to make a statement. Then after we have dealt with the evidence or with the information submitted by the parties to the Chamber, we'll give an opportunity to the parties for their closing argument, as far as sentencing is concerned. If there would be any questions by the Judges, they can be either put to you immediately or at the very end of this hearing. May I then first invite the Prosecution to make the -- some opening remarks. I had in mind that the opening remarks should be completed in approximately 50 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours, counsel. Your Honours, the purpose of my opening remarks is to provide you with an outline of the evidence the Prosecution will adduce this afternoon. I will also identify those issues that the Prosecution submits are of particular relevance to this sentencing hearing. And lastly, Your Honours, I will touch on some of the relevant sentencing factors where the Prosecution and Defence have different views. Before I address those matters, however, I would like to briefly discuss the incidents and events that led us to today's sentencing hearing. On the 21st of August, 1992, Darko Mrdja and other members of a special unit of the Prijedor Police, known as the "Intervention Squad" participated in the murder of approximately 200 non-Serb civilians at a location called Koricanske Stijene or the Koricani Cliffs on Mount Vlasic. These predominantly Muslim men and a few boys had been passengers on a convoy of non-Serbs out of Prijedor in the direction of Travnik. As Your Honours will hear from our witnesses today, miraculously 12 men managed to survive the massacre. Darko Mrdja was indicted by this Tribunal on the 16th of April, 2002. He was arrested in Prijedor on the 13th of June,2002, transferred to The Hague the next day. At his Initial Appearance before the Tribunal on 17 June 2002, he plead not guilty to the charges in the indictment. On the 24th of July, 2003, five days before his trial was set to begin, and pursuant to an agreement between the parties, Darko Mrdja changed his plea to guilty to Count 2 of the indictment and Count 3 of the indictment, as Your Honour mentioned earlier. At that hearing, the Prosecution moved to dismiss Count 1, and subsequently filed an amended indictment. Darko Mrdja's guilty pleas were accepted by this Chamber and findings of guilt were entered for Counts 2 and 3 of the indictment. Your Honour, in our written submissions and in our presentation and through our witnesses today, the Prosecution has endeavoured to identify the issues that are critical for Your Honours in determining what is a just sentence for Darko Mrdja. We have relied upon the Statute of the Tribunal, the Tribunal's Rules of Procedure and Evidence, and upon the jurisprudence of this Tribunal. We have made detailed written submissions about the factors that are relevant for your consideration. Those factors are: First, the gravity of the offence; Second, the individual circumstances of the accused; Third, aggravating or mitigating circumstances, and; Fourth, the general practices regarding sentencing in the former Yugoslavia. In our oral submissions later today, we will identify some of these factors where we differ from the Defence. We will also, in our oral submissions, attempt to clarify the Prosecution's position with respect to the gravity of the crime at issue here, in which convictions have been entered for violation of the laws or customs of war, as well as for crimes against humanity. Today the Prosecution will call two witnesses to give evidence relevant to sentencing. In putting forward these witnesses, it is not the Prosecution's intent to sensationalise or dramatise the events at Koricanske Stijene. The gravity of this crime requires no embellishment. The witnesses you will hear from, one survivor of the massacre and one representative from Bosnian Victim's Support Organisation, will attempt to put the event and its lasting effect on the victims and their family members into an appropriate context for Your Honours. The first witness, Mr. Midhet Mujkanovic, is a survivor of the massacre at Koricanske Stijene. Mr. Mujkanovic will recount for Your Honours the events of 21 August 1992. He will describe the physical condition of the victims and how many of the victims had been detained at the notorious prison camps, Omarska and Keraterm, in Prijedor. He will describe his remarkable story of survival and the aftermath of the massacre. He will also explain how this incident has left lasting effects on him. Mr. Mujkanovic's testimony will highlight for Your Honours both the gravity of the crime and the vulnerability of the victims. Given the large scale of the massacre at Koricanske Stijene, it is not possible to put forward all the stories from the victim's families. We propose to give Your Honours a summary of the victim's stories through our second Prosecution witness, Ms. Seida Karabasic. Ms. Karabasic is the president of the Izvor Association of Prijedor Women, an organisation headquartered in Sanski Most and dedicated to finding missing persons and working with the victims and family members from the conflict in Bosnia. Ms. Karabasic will testify on behalf of the victims and their surviving family members, many of whom she has personally met and worked with. She will explain the desires of the family members, that the perpetrators of this crime be brought to justice and that the bodies of the victims be recovered. We will play some portions of the video from a memorial service --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel kindly slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: I apologise to the interpreters. We will play some portions of a video from a memorial service at Koricanske Stijene from 21 August 2002, the tenth anniversary of the massacre. Ms. Karabasic will identify for Your Honours some of the family members and relate to you their stories. We submit that the victims and the family members' stories will assist Your Honours in assessing the gravity of the crime. Finally, Mr. Tieger will make oral submissions about the factors that I have mentioned. Rather than file written responses to the sentencing briefs, the parties have discussed their positions and will make their responses orally. The Prosecution respectfully disagrees with the Defence with respect to a number of proposed mitigating factors. Among the factors on which we take issue with the Defence position are the proper evaluation of remorse, vulnerability of the victims, the impact of the psychological expert report, and the interplay between duress and superior orders. We will also use this opportunity to clarify for the Chamber the Prosecution's position with respect to the gravity of the offences and whether one charge should be given greater weight. We will also submit today an amended annex to the amended indictment filed on 4 August 2003. The Prosecution's investigative efforts on this case have continued throughout the proceedings, and we have been able to correct the annex to the indictment, which contains a list of the victims from the Koricanske massacre. Your Honours, we will also request that a short portion of our submissions be made in private session. Mr. Tieger will address the Chamber about the issues outlined above and will frame for Your Honours how those factors, in addition to the evidence adduced today, and the statements submitted with our brief, support the Prosecution's recommendation of an appropriate sentence for Darko Mrdja. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The request is whether the Prosecution would be willing to share the rostrums with the Defence, since there is no additional one available. I already now indicate that the Chamber will consider whether an amendment to one of the annexes to the indictment could still be filed at this late stage where the Chamber has already accepted the plea. Nevertheless, the Chamber would like to be informed on whether, for example, if you want to strike out names of the list that by mistake are there, I think it's important that at least this is known to the public, apart from what our decision will be on whether it's admissible or not, to -- to change the annex, to make a new amended annex. That's, in this stage of the procedure, I would say, usually it would not be admissible. But if there's any -- any other thing you'd like to submit in that respect, we'll hear from you. Then, Mr. Wachenheim, I invite you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WACHENHEIM
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours, learned colleagues from the Office of the Prosecutor. In my introductory remarks, I would like to do two things: First, to give a short overview of the arguments the Defence has presented in its sentencing brief for consideration of this Honourable Chamber in order to assist you in finding, to use the words of the Todorovic Court, the sentence that fits the crime; and second, since the Defence is not going to present any live witnesses today but it has tendered into evidence a number of documents and nine written witnesses' statements, it wants to give you an indication what is contained in them. In its brief, the Defence has pointed you to the general sentencing considerations of retribution and deterrence but also to the importance of rehabilitation. In our final argument, you will be given a detailed assessment of the gravity of the crime and an analysis of what elements of the crime are already subsumed in the gravity of the committed offence and, therefore, cannot be considered twice. In this context, we will also comment on whether there are any aggravating factors to be considered by this Honourable Chamber. As the centerpiece of the Defence arguments in the brief, we extensively have dealt with the mitigating factors in this case as they are; Mr. Mrdja's cooperation with the Office of the Prosecutor, his guilty plea, and his expression of remorse. Lead counsel will discuss the notion of duress as a mitigating factor and the findings of the expert witness, Professor Gallwitz, in this respect and as to the personality of the accused as they are contained in his report of 13 October 2003. Based on national jurisprudence, the Defence has introduced two new mitigating factors for this Honourable Chamber to consider; namely, first, a long time lapse between the commission of the criminal act and the beginning of a trial and; second, the fact that it constitutes a particular hardship on a defendant if he has to serve his sentence in a country that is particularly foreign to him. The Defence in its brief has discussed Mr. Mrdja's personal circumstances before and after the war and has presented as evidence the statement of the United Nations Detention Unit's prison warden confirming that the conduct of Mr. Mrdja while being detained has been cooperative and respectful. We also have introduced witnesses' statements, the contents of which I want to very quickly bring to your attention, and this then will be the end of my opening remarks. I will follow the order of Annex B of our sentencing brief. First, in the statement of Dragana Mrdja, Darko Mrdja's wife, in very moving words, describes the extremely tight economic situation of the couple since their living together in the year 1997, the severe medical condition of their son Nikola, and the almost disastrous emotional and financial situation that she and their two children have to deal with on a daily basis since Darko Mrdja's arrest. Second, the statement of Darko Mrdja's younger sister, also named Dragana Mrdja, describes the working-class family background, the fact that before the war Darko Mrdja had social contacts with all ethnic groups in Bosnia, and the change the sister noticed in her brother during the war and after the Koricanske Stijene incident in particular, finally, the fact that right after this event, he left the police and returned back to his military unit. Three, the statement of protected Witness WIS, a Bosniak from Tukovi, the village where Mrdja is from. He has known Darko Mrdja and his entire family from before the war. He describes the relationship he had had with him as uncomplicated and without ethnic bias. After the war, Mr. Mrdja and the witness got together more frequently, and again the witness did not notice any ethnic prejudice against Muslims. The fourth witness's statement is that of Roman Ostojic. He mentions Darko Mrdja's good sportsmanship as a fisherman and his correct behaviour towards citizens of other ethnic groups. The witness, as the owner of a cafe where the accused was a frequent guest, was able to observe Darko Mrdja regularly. Fifth, Goran Zgonjanin also describes Mrdja as a good and fair sportsman who, when in company, was pleasant and entertaining and in the presence of the witness has never shown any ethnic bias. Six is Dusko Bubalo. He describes the way Mrdja was arrested by SFOR, that he was severely beaten and that he did not resist and actually had no chance to resist his arrest. Seven is the statement of Damir Ceranic. He was Darko Mrdja's passenger in the car when both were arrested by SFOR. He describes the circumstances of this arrest and confirms that there was no resistance on Darko Mrdja's part. Furthermore, Ceranic also confirms that in everyday life he never noticed any ethnic prejudices with Darko Mrdja. The eighth statement is that of Damir Cankovic, who has known the accused for 16 years, confirms that Mrdja has not been hiding in any way before his arrest, and he explains the reasons why Darko Mrdja was carrying the witness's pistol at the time of his arrest. The last statement I want to deal with is that of Ostoja Barasin, former commander in the rank of a colonel of 5th Kozarska Brigade and Darko Mrdja's superior in the military police. Colonel Barasin describes Mrdja's work as a military policeman as having been reliable and consistent without any showing of ethnic intolerance, and the witness states that Darko Mrdja was brave and that his conduct as a policeman never gave rise to any complaints. Those, Your Honours, were my introductory remarks, and I thank you for your attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Wachenheim. Perhaps before we continue and before we give an opportunity to the Prosecution to call their witnesses, I'd like to raise one issue with you. This sentencing hearing takes place on the basis of the guilty plea of Mr. Mrdja, and the Chamber was somewhat troubled by what the psychologist describes as the factual basis on which he, at least, drafted his psychological report. Let me just give you a small example. In the plea agreement, it says that "Mr. Mrdja selected men of military age with the awareness and expectation that these men would be killed." I think it even says that he personally selected these men. But if I look at the psychological report, which describes that the factual basis for this found in the -- what Mr. Mrdja has told the psychologist, then he says -- or at least, it reads that "While selecting, upon the request of Mr. Mrdja, he was told at the time that there would be an exchange of prisoners," which is quite a different -- quite a different course of events, where the plea agreement says, "He selected men with the awareness and expectation that these men would be killed." He says, "I selected them and I asked for information and they told me that there would be an exchange of prisoners." Well, that's not the only difference. For example, in the plea agreement, it says that Mr. Mrdja personally selected. In -- to the psychologist, at least in the report, it says: "Some people were chosen." By whom is totally unclear. On the basis of what criteria also is perfectly unclear. So also if we look at the plea agreement, we see that Mr. Mrdja participated in the shooting and killing of the victims. And if I look at what he told the psychologist, I see that it -- it gives the impression as if he was shooting at a person or persons who tried to escape without saying whether he hit someone. He only said that he targeted to the right part of the -- of the body. But then he said, "I was shooting without aiming at people." That's the next step. And then finally he says that "During the time he held the gun in his hands, approximately 10 people were hit by bullets." How has the Chamber to understand this course of events, where it seems that a picture is created that Mr. Mrdja was standing there with his weapon and while he was standing there, ten people were killed? By whom? Not by Mr. Mrdja; Mr. Mrdja, who did not aim at persons? It's -- it's not clear whether in his statement on facts to the psychologist Mr. Mrdja did not, in fact, say that he did not plead guilty of murder. A murder requires intent to kill someone. Could you please clarify this before we continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. WACHENHEIM
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. But my lead counsel indicated to me that he would like to answer your question, with your permission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course. It's entirely up to you who does.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we also noticed those ambiguities in this report. Unfortunately, we don't have any transcript from the interview what held Professor Gallwitz with our client. He spent, as far as we know, one morning with him. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The report says seven hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Okay, seven hours. It's something more than one morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: But Mr. Mrdja himself, he gave a statement regarding this event a couple of times; at least two times to the Office of the Prosecutor and once, what I will consider in the closing session. So Mr. Mrdja firmly relies on his statements. I don't know how Professor Gallwitz had such conclusions and how did Mr. Mrdja said what -- what the professor said in his report, but -- but that makes us to -- to some questions which we cannot really respond. We -- with all respects, we -- we have -- we respect the Trial Chamber decision not to interfere in that -- in that -- with that witness. We don't -- we didn't have any contact with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I just interrupt you. Do I understand you well that you say that the Defence takes distance from wherever the psychological report gives a cause of events attributed by the psychologist to Mr. Mrdja but -- at least, it gives a course of events that's different. You take distance from that as far as it's not consistent with the statement of facts in the -- in the plea agreement? Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Actually, Your Honour, we must say that we cannot completely have distance of that report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I'm just saying you take distance to the extent that the facts as described by the psychologist are inconsistent with the content of the plea agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, exactly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then that's, at least, clear to us. You will understand that this might have some consequences for the evaluation of the psychological report as well, since the psychologist based his opinion on the facts as he describes them to be presented to him. But we'll deal with that later on. But this, of course, causes a -- an additional problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We are aware of that. And we are sorry for that. But that's how things are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Then thank you very much for your -- for your introduction, your opening remarks, Mr. Wachenheim; for your answer to our question, Mr. Dimitrijevic. I think we have come to the point where the Prosecution could call his first witness, which I understand is Midhet Mujkanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mujkanovic, I take it? May I also take it that you understand me in a language -- that you hear me in a language you understand? Yes. The Court invites you to make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth when you testify in this court. The text is being handed to you now by the usher. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please be seated, Mr. Mujkanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, is it agreed upon the parties that there will be no cross-examination, or did I understand it well, or -- it's just examination-in-chief, or ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think it's fair to say there's no expectation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No expectation. So, of course, you could not exclude for certain prior to that, but the parties, yes, are not -- have not agreed that there will certainly be cross-examination. Has not been claimed by the Defence in this case, I understand. Then please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Examined by Mr. Tieger:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. And thank you for being here today. Can we begin by having you state your full name, please.

utterances.speaker: MIDHET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Midhet Mujkanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where were you born and raised?

utterances.speaker: MIDHET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: I was born in Jakupovici on the 2nd of September, 1964, Prijedor municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you living in Prijedor municipality in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIDHET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I lived in the municipality of Prijedor at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your occupation, Mr. Mujkanovic?

utterances.speaker: MIDHET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: At the time, I did not have an occupation as such. We had some land. I worked the land. I was jobless. I used to work in Slovenia as a plumber, and I was made redundant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mujkanovic, we will be asking you about the events of August 21st, 1992. But before I inquire about that day, will briefly ask you to describe some of the background events that brought you to that day. Were you in your village or at home when the conflict began?

utterances.speaker: MIDHET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was. I was in my village at home, yes, when the conflict began.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your village shelled?

utterances.speaker: MIDHET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was shelled from all sides intensely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you and your neighbours leave your homes and surrender to the Bosnian Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: MIDHET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I surrendered after two days. I did. I came to Kamicani. We hid in the forest by Kozarac. So we were between Kozarac and Kamicani. As for the others, some people stayed in the village and surrendered to the Serbs immediately. I surrendered after a day or two. So that we were everywhere in Kozarac area. Many people were in other places, in Trnopolje and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where were you taken after you surrendered?

utterances.speaker: MIDHET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: From the Kozarac station, we were taken to Keraterm, in Prijedor. I surrendered in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long were you in Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: MIDHET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: I stayed there a night or two.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you taken after that?

utterances.speaker: MIDHET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: To Omarska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mr. Mujkanovic, approximately how long were you held in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: MIDHET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, approximately more than two months. Two months and ten days. And since I was declared to be a civilian, I and some 600 to 700 people were sent to Trnopolje, because they concluded that I was not a soldier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you briefly describe your physical condition after you were released from Omarska and sent to Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MIDHET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: I was in a really bad situation. I had lost a lot of weight. I didn't weigh more than 53 kilogrammes. And both in physical and mental sense I was a broken man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 21st of August, 1992 did you and others board a convoy of trucks and buses that departed Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: MIDHET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did that convoy consist of men, women, and children?

utterances.speaker: MIDHET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what ethnicity were the passengers in that convoy?

utterances.speaker: MIDHET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Those of us who were at the camp were mostly Muslims. Perhaps there were some Croats. The Serbs and their authorities were the ones who organised the convoy. Most of the people were civilians, and it was mostly Muslims who lived in the Kozarac area. And this convoy was a means of getting out of that situation for them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there other men who had been released from either Omarska or Keraterm and whose physical condition resembled your own?

utterances.speaker: MIDHET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember that. I don't remember people on that convoy. The situation was such that it was very difficult to watch it. It is possible that some people who had come from Omarska were in that convoy too.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to show the witness an exhibit. And I'd like this marked, please, as a Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, the suggestion of the Chamber is that you mark the exhibits with S numbers, so it would then be S1 the original will then be marked by Madam Registrar. So S1 will then be a map with the Trnopolje-Vlasic route on it with the number 02166228.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mujkanovic, taking a look at Exhibit S1, does that depict, to the best of your recollection, the route that the convoy took on the 21st of August, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIDHET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it does show realistically that route. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mujkanovic, during the course of the convoy's progression from Trnopolje in the direction of Travnik, can you give us some indication of the manner in which the passengers were treated by the guards on the convoy?

utterances.speaker: MIDHET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, at the time, I didn't get an impression that they were threatening us directly. I didn't see anything to that effect. However, there was one situation that seemed strange to me. When we stopped some 50 kilometres from Banja Luka, after we had travelled 50 kilometres, they allowed us to have a break. We got out and drank water from the stream. Then all of the guards gathered in a circle. And at that time it crossed my mind that the situation wasn't really a hopeful one. All of them, the drivers and the guards or the bodyguards, as we called them, they all got together. They sat next to each other, talking. I don't know what they were talking about. But in the meantime, every time we passed by a military facility, they would start yelling and not allow us to look around.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mujkanovic, had the passengers in the convoy attempted to bring some of their possessions - money, jewellery - with them during the -- during their departure from Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MIDHET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: It is possible that some people had some valuables if that had not been looted prior to that. Every time they took custody of our people, they would take their valuables away from them. So what could we have on us? Not much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were there similar attempts to take whatever valuables the passengers had on this convoy?

utterances.speaker: MIDHET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. When they started disembarking us from the bus and they told us to move from one bus to the other, at that point they wanted us to turn over all the valuables we had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mujkanovic, at some point during that convoy, were you removed from the bus on which you had been a passenger?

utterances.speaker: MIDHET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we travelled, and it's hard to say how long we travelled from Banja Luka to that particular point where we stopped. It could have been two hours. But on one occasion they stopped the buses at a site that was not familiar to me, because I had never travelled that route before and I didn't know the road well. So we stopped, and they started threatening us. They told us we had to leave buses. And I saw that some men were hesitant; they didn't want to leave. And the guard was insistent and angry, demanding them to leave. And I tried to get away, to avoid that situation. Some people that sat next to me were taken off the bus, and then the guard came and closed the door. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where were you and the other men who had been taken off the buses placed?

utterances.speaker: MIDHET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Then we were transferred to another bus. When we got to the other bus, we were packed very tightly, like sardines in a can. People were desperate. They were frightened. They started yelling at us. They wanted valuables from us, money, and so on. They told us that we had nothing to worry about, that they would exchange us for their fighters. That's how it was. However, I felt some tension. I had a premonition that something bad was going to happen to us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Once you and the others were packed into that bus, where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: MIDHET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: They waited until the civilians left, women, children, and the elderly, until they left for Travnik. And where they took us from there is something that I really can't tell you. I don't know whether we drove for 20 minutes or we remained in that same spot. I really can't tell you that. But I know that at one point they stopped the buses. So I think that they did drive us somewhere else, yes. So they stopped buses, they ordered us to get off buses, they ordered us to look down, they wouldn't let us look around, so that I remember -- I remember that they took me in front of the bus and then they took us back, and then they lined us up at an edge, where things happened later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mujkanovic, I'm going to ask you to look at a photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I'm going to ask that this be marked as Exhibit S2, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mujkanovic, first I'm going to ask you if you recognise the site depicted in the photograph. And is that the site where the buses were taken?

utterances.speaker: MIDHET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: I think it is. I think that this is the site. I'm a hundred per cent sure that this is the site.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mujkanovic, using that photograph, if it assists you in describing the events, can you tell the Judges, please, what happened after you and the others were taken to this site.

utterances.speaker: MIDHET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: When we were brought to that site, they lined us up. So they took us first to the front of the bus, then back behind the bus, and then at one point they ordered us to turn, and then they brought us to the very edge, the very edge shown there, next to the abyss, facing the abyss. Then people started screaming, yelling. I knew right away that something bad was going to happen. And I can't remember to this day whether somebody pushed me or instinctively I jumped myself. I just know that I leaped into the abyss. And then I heard people who started crying automatically, and they were shooting, even throwing hand grenades. When I became conscious, I realised that through some incredible luck I was not injured. I still couldn't believe the situation I was in. Then I saw something in front of me. There was a rock. And it immediately occurred to me that I could use that rock as a shelter. I was a bit away from that rock. In front of me I saw dead people. And that was my only chance, my only chance. I had to do that. So I took a body of a man and I covered myself with that human body. I sheltered myself with it. And then I tried to crawl to the rock. And at that moment I heard somebody yell from above, "Somebody's moving down there." And then they started shooting. So the dead man, whose name I don't know to this day, saved my life. The entire time they shot at anybody who cried for help. They had no mercy. I remained there for perhaps an hour throughout that time, while that was taking place. As I lay there, I tried to see where I was. I saw dead people around me, wounded people around me, but I remember that moment that there was a guard there who couldn't have been older than 20 years, and he said, "You Turks got what you deserved." He was not more than 20. He laughed at the agony that we were experiencing. So that after those two hours, I heard as the buses came back from the Travnik direction - I don't know how far they went - and then I heard somebody say, "Everything is over. Everything is over. There are no more living there." They started their buses and headed back to Prijedor. It was already dusk at the time. It could have been 7.30. I got up and started running. I even believed that I had been surrendered. I was experiencing this great fear, and I even tried to kill myself. I jumped off the rock. I was completely desolate. However, I managed to get some control over myself, and I headed for the forest. I spent the first night in the forest, not far from the site, perhaps 600 metres away. There was a large forest there, and I slept on a tree the first night. The second evening, the second day, I also wandered around. I hallucinated a lot. That's all I can say about that event.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a couple of additional questions related to that, Mr. Mujkanovic. Did you encounter any other survivors during the time you were in that area, before you were captured?

utterances.speaker: MIDHET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: On the following day, while I was wandering around, [redacted]

utterances.speaker: MIDHET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: [redacted]I don't remember that person's name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand that you were captured after the second night you spent in that area. Where were you taken after you were apprehended?

utterances.speaker: MIDHET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, they took me to Skender Vakuf, where I was interrogated by a major. I think that was his rank. He was a major or a captain. He was greying. He was between 55 and 60 years old. He beat me around the head. He said, "You're a lucky man. You survived." Then I found this Suljo Kahrimanovic. He was one of the first persons to be brought in. We had a cell there. And then Sivac came, Medo Sivac, someone who also survived, from a place near my place of birth. They're all people -- most of them are from the Kozarac area. Then Bahrija Jakupovic came, a neighbour of mine. And there was another man from Sivac I can't remember his name. He also appeared. And then from there, from Skender Vakuf, they transferred us to the hospital in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you briefly describe the way you were treated in the hospital in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MIDHET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: In the hospital, well, they treated us worse than livestock. Anyone could come at any time to beat us, to provoke us, to do whatever they wanted to do to us, everything. They could do everything. One night they beat me with cables. They would beat us with cables, and they would order you to take your shirt off. When they hit you with a cable, this is a little ironic, it's a little sad. I would rather have had a policeman beat me for three days than to be beaten with a cable twice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mujkanovic, I understand after your release from the hospital you were eventually returned to Trnopolje camp and then left Prijedor on a convoy that left Bosnia. Let me ask you now if you can explain to the Judges whether you have any lingering physical or emotional effects that you attribute to the events of August 21st, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MIDHET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't have any physical effects. But in terms of psychological effects, yes. I don't sleep well. The job I have is one that I like a lot, but I don't know whether I'll manage to continue working. I have great difficulty in concentrating. This has left permanent traces, permanent consequences. And unfortunately, it is difficult to find a remedy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mujkanovic, I want to ask you one last question based on -- on something you said to me when we talked earlier. In spite of all that you endured, can I ask you whether or not you have hope for the future in Bosnia-Herzegovina, hope for the relationships between the ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: MIDHET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, my vision is that after all those conflicts, reason should be victorious. My vision is that people should start communicating normally again. But there is one thing that we can't conceal. We can't conceal those crimes. Each side should apologise and say that they are aware of the facts. Until the war criminals are at large and still have parties of their own, so long as that is the case, one can't expect there to be a real and permanent peace. We're talking about the Balkans, after all. But I hope that reason will prevail and that the future will be better. I sincerely hope so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Mujkanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. Mr. Mujkanovic, you have been called as a witness for the Prosecution. I have to give an opportunity to the Defence also to put questions to you, and I understand that the Defence will fully understand what your position is, having been taken back to the events of August 1992. Is there any need to examine the witness, to -- I wouldn't use the word cross-examining but to put any questions to the witness, Mr. Dimitrijevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, the Defence will not have questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge El Mahdi would like to put a question to you. Questioned by the Court: JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] It's just a matter of clarification, a minor question I would like to put to the witness. When you spoke about the incident in the buses, you were in one of the buses and you said with regard to that incident - and I'll quote you in English - [In English] "They waited until the civilians left, women, children, and the elderly, until they left for Travnik." [Interpretation] What I would like to know is were you considered to be civilians or were you combatants? Because at the beginning you said that you had a job as a plumber and that you were a civilian. So I'm a little confused on this point, and I would like to hear your comments, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIDHET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, what could I say? That I was a soldier in the former Yugoslavia? I didn't have a weapon. How could I have been a soldier? How could I have played a military role in all of this? Naturally I was a civilian. I considered myself to be a civilian. I had no weapons of any kind. And I'll swear this on the Bible. If only I had had a weapon, I would have been able to defend myself. But how could I have done that? JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness. [In English] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Mujkanovic, since I have no further questions to you, I would like to thank you for having come to The Hague and to have answered all questions put to you. This Chamber fully understands that it might not have been easy for you to be taken back to an event, to a day which has had, as you told us, quite some impact on your life. Therefore, I again would like to thank you. And you are excused. Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I think this would be an appropriate moment to have a short break. Since the Chamber thinks that it could be possible to finish by today, we'd like to make the breaks not long to start with. So I'd like to adjourn until ten minutes to 4.00, for 20 minutes. I then take it that after the break that you'll call your next witness and that we'll then continue with a statement of Mr. Mrdja or whatever the Defence would like to submit at that moment before coming to closing arguments. I'm also aware that you have asked previously for just a short break after the oral statement of Mr. Mrdja, but could you do without, or -- because it fits not that well in our schedule. If you need a break at a certain moment, please let us know. Then we can consider it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I think we can adjust to the Court's preference with regard to the breaks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll adjourn until ten minutes to 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, is the Prosecution ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Resch. Madam registrar left the courtroom already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Ms. Karabasic, I take it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. From your reaction, I understand that you can hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Karabasic, before giving evidence in this court, I would like to invite you to make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text will be handed out to you now by the usher. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Karabasic. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You'll be examined by counsel for the Prosecution. Perhaps the usher could help you, because if you keep it that way, it would easily fall off, the earphones. That's a common experience. If it's uncomfortable, please seek the assistance of the usher. Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Resch.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Examined by Mr. Resch:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, ma'am. Could you please state your name for the record.

utterances.speaker: SEIDA KARABASIC
utterances.text: Seida Karabasic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ms. Karabasic, could you please tell us when you were born and where, please.

utterances.speaker: SEIDA KARABASIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 14th of June, 1965, in Kozarusa, the Prijedor municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For how long did you live in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: SEIDA KARABASIC
utterances.text: Up until April 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened in April of 1992 that caused you to leave Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: SEIDA KARABASIC
utterances.text: War had already broken out in Slovenia and Croatia, and war was being prepared in Bosnia and Herzegovina too. The army passed through our village and opened fire. Many Serbian soldiers would go to the battlefield in Croatia and would return with a lot of weapons and they would open fire at night. So the inhabitants of that place were afraid. I had a small child, a five-year-old child. And before that, I had a tragedy in my family, so my parents wanted me to leave so that I didn't have to experience the war there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that tragedy was your husband's accidental death?

utterances.speaker: SEIDA KARABASIC
utterances.text: Yes. My husband died in the course of his duty. He had an accident. He received an electric shock.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You and your young daughter then went to Croatia and eventually Slovenia?

utterances.speaker: SEIDA KARABASIC
utterances.text: Yes. I left by bus with a lot of other women and children. The route we took wasn't a normal route. It was a macadam route, because you couldn't use the road that was usually used to get to Croatia. And during that trip, the troops would stop us and inspect us. We had quite a few unpleasant experiences.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in January of 1996, you returned to Bosnia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEIDA KARABASIC
utterances.text: Yes. At the end of the war, I returned to Sanski Most and continued to live there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Chamber about the organisation you and ten other people founded, headquartered in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: SEIDA KARABASIC
utterances.text: When I returned to Sanski Most or, rather, a place near Sanski Most, a place called Lusci Palanka, a lot of displaced people returned, a lot of Bosniaks from Prijedor returned, and I was among them. And we women, single mothers, we felt it necessary to organise ourselves and to help other women and orphans and the elderly, so we had the idea of founding a non-governmental organisation, and we did that in June 1996. We founded this organisation, which was registered in the high court in Bihac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the name of that organisation is the Izvor Association of Prijedor Women?

utterances.speaker: SEIDA KARABASIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the original president of Izvor?

utterances.speaker: SEIDA KARABASIC
utterances.text: The first president of Izvor was Munira Fazlic. She spent the entire wartime period in Bosnia. And the women who returned from outside felt in some way that we should honour her in this way, give her this honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Ms. Fazlic have any connection to the massacre that occurred at Koricanske Stijene?

utterances.speaker: SEIDA KARABASIC
utterances.text: Yes, she did. Ms. Fazlic passed through some time before the massacre in Koricanske Stijene. Her husband and her husband's two brothers remained in Trnopolje. Munira Fazlic, like all the other citizens who had been expelled through Skender Vakuf towards the free area of Travnik -- well, she told me that every day she looked in the direction of Vlasic in hope that her husband would come.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to Ms. Fazlic's husband?

utterances.speaker: SEIDA KARABASIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Her husband left with the others in the group, and he was separated with his brother on Vlasic. There was a group of 250 people there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was the convoy on 21 August 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEIDA KARABASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Izvor Association, please tell us about the association's work in compiling the Prijedor book of the missing.

utterances.speaker: SEIDA KARABASIC
utterances.text: Our association was founded in order to help women, single mothers, orphans, and the elderly. But when we started working and in the course of conducting certain projects, we found out that on the whole these families' greatest problems concerned the fact that family members of theirs had gone missing. And although we tried to assist them with -- by providing them with goods that they didn't have, we found out through conversations with them that the most important thing for them was for us to find out where their family members who had gone missing or who had been killed were actually located. So as early as 1997 we started compiling information on people who were missing. We organised ourselves in several places in the territory of the Federation by founding teams in those places, and these teams would work on gathering information. By using the media, the radio, the television and the newspapers, we would inform people -- we would inform people that we wanted them to contact us and to provide us with information on the whereabouts of family members of theirs who had gone missing, to provide us with photographs so that we could gather all this information and use this information in the course of our work to locate the missing people, and we issued a first edition. Only 200 copies were printed. And there are about 2.700 persons included in this list of people who had gone missing. We distributed these copies throughout the world, in places where our people had taken refuge, so that they could also compile information on those who had gone missing, because most of the people from Prijedor had been expelled and they now live in over 100 countries worldwide. So we'd get information back. We'd gather a lot of photographs. We would correct the errors contained in the first edition. And in the year 2000, we published a book on those missing from Prijedor, and this includes the list of the 2.700 people missing and the list of this name -- of these people included 122 children.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you personally as part of your work, gathering names for the Prijedor book of the missing, you met with a number of families who had lost a family member at Koricanske Stijene on 21 August; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEIDA KARABASIC
utterances.text: Yes. I met those family members, and it's important to stress that those families had a particular problem. Many people went missing at one location. They didn't have any information. No one was trying to find out the truth about what had happened. Up until 1997 and to this very day many of these people are still persuaded that their family members are still alive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe you first had contact with someone who lost a family member at Koricani in 1992, while you were in Slovenia. Could you -- could you please tell us about that person.

utterances.speaker: SEIDA KARABASIC
utterances.text: It was a woman from my neighbourhood. She had gone to Slovenia. And we took her in. We -- she lived with us until she could find some other place. She had two children, and she told us about the event. On that day, he was at Koricanske Stijene, and her brother was separated with another group on that day. And her father-in-law was separated too. But she pointed out that her brother had left from Trnopolje because she had asked him to do so. She had persuaded him to do so. She then asked the then-commander of the camp, Slobodan Kuruzovic for permission, and he gave him authority to leave. She was -- he was her youngest brother and she would cry every day. She felt guilty because she had called him on that day and encouraged him to leave. She said that it was very difficult for her to meet their parents because she couldn't look them in the eyes. She didn't know what to tell them about the whereabouts of their son.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the year 2002, your organisation organised a memorial for the tenth anniversary. Do you know if the families prior to this anniversary memorial had had an opportunity to visit the site of the massacre at Koricani?

utterances.speaker: SEIDA KARABASIC
utterances.text: No. None of the families went there up until that date. It wasn't possible to go there, because it was at some distance and it wasn't safe to go there. We tried to get some people to take us to the site, but everyone refused to do so. They all refused to do so. So we had the idea of organising a visit to that location, because in the course of our work we had realised that those families wanted to confront the truth, because they were still convinced that their family members were alive and they could not even imagine how this event had happened. No one could believe that there were no survivors. That's why we wanted to organise that visit. We wanted to take them to the site so that they could see for themselves. And we also wanted to draw attention to incident in question, because no one spoke about Koricanske Stijene. We wanted the local authorities and we wanted the international community to be put under pressure. We wanted to pressurise them and to try and get someone to do something about this matter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe you commissioned a video to be made of the visit that the -- the people made to Koricani on the 21st of August, 2002.

utterances.speaker: SEIDA KARABASIC
utterances.text: Yes. We asked a young man, an amateur who was from our town, to help us and to record the footage on that day, so that we would be able to send videotapes to the families living abroad so that they could see for themselves that we had gone to visit the site.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time I'd like to play a clip of -- a number of clips from the video. This -- we have this on CD, which we'll tender as Prosecution Exhibit S3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] That will be exhibited as S3. Do I take it that the translated text has been disclosed already to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: I believe it has, Your Honour. And actually, the transcript of the text will just be at the fifth clip, and I'll notify the booth when we'll have a short portion of the transcript translated.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The transcript will be S3.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: I believe we should be able to see this, this video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: If you could just pause it there for a moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ms. Karabasic, I'll ask you a few questions while the video is playing but we can also let it run during some other portions. If you could just tell the Court what this first location is, and we can go ahead and let the video run.

utterances.speaker: SEIDA KARABASIC
utterances.text: This is the location in Kozarac, the starting point from which the convoy with buses started out. So we had to find a place where we would gather at and start from because of security and other issues.

utterances.speaker: SEIDA KARABASIC
utterances.text: These people here are waiting for the bus to start out to Koricanske Stijene.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately how many buses did you organise for that day?

utterances.speaker: SEIDA KARABASIC
utterances.text: In the very beginning, when we talked about organising this event, we didn't know that so many people would come. We planned for several buses. And we simply wanted to see how many people would sign up for this event. Several other NGOs assisted us, NGOs that participated in organising this event with us. So in their areas, they compiled lists of people who signed up to attend. Several days after that, we saw that a lot of people had signed up and we had to find additional buses. Some calls were made even on the last night before the event. People called us even at midnight, saying that they would like to come. However, we did not have a sufficient number of buses. In the end, nine buses and several private vehicles left Kozarac headed in that direction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe this is a video of the people initially walking to the site. Can you describe the atmosphere on the way to the site.

utterances.speaker: SEIDA KARABASIC
utterances.text: While we travelled from Kozarac to Vlasic, people simply couldn't wait to get there. I was on one of the buses with people there, and when we got there, we had to stop at a certain point because buses couldn't continue on. So we disembarked and continued on foot. People were in a hurry, and one could feel that they expected they would find something there, that something would be awaiting for them there, and they couldn't wait to get there. It is very difficult to describe that to somebody who hasn't experienced that, who hasn't been around those people. They looked at the rocks where there were a lot of policemen, and many of them who had passed there in 1992 felt a certain fear, as if they were living through that again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were the reactions of the family members upon initially seeing the cliffs?

utterances.speaker: SEIDA KARABASIC
utterances.text: When they came to the site and when they were told that that was the site, mothers fell to their knees, started crying. Some of them wanted to leap into the abyss, and we had to keep them from doing that. They were saying, "Look where my child met his end." It was terrible to look down into the abyss. One couldn't even see where it ended. These people were expecting to find something there. They were expecting to see something down there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the video, the man -- we saw a man just pointing down the cliffs. Do you know what he was pointing at?

utterances.speaker: SEIDA KARABASIC
utterances.text: The man is pointing down. He's trying to see the remains. I don't know whether he in fact saw some bodily remains, but perhaps of this great desire of his it seemed to him that he had seen something that could be used as evidence. Some people saw bullet traces there. I don't know whether they dated back from 1992. However, they pointed to those traces and said, "This is what was used to kill our children."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately how many people went to the visit that day?

utterances.speaker: SEIDA KARABASIC
utterances.text: There were over 500 people. Although, not all of those who wished to come could come. A lot of people came from the abroad, from Sweden, Germany, Denmark, Switzerland. Some people came through other organisations involved in these matters, and they came and joined us there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't hear the audio, so we'll just keep proceeding as we have been.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall the --

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] Ladies and gentlemen, dear brothers and sisters, esteemed guests. We've gathered here today at the mountain of Vlasic through which ten years ago the members of the police, the military and the paramilitary forces of Republika Srpska - or as it was then called, the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina - expelled tens of thousands of non-Serbs, citizens of Prijedor and the surrounding villages. The reason, however, for us being here at Koricanske Stijene is to recall one of the most horrifying crimes committed against us, residents of Prijedor. On 21st of August, 1992, exactly ten years ago today, they brought 253 of our fellow citizens right here, to the edge of this abyss. These are the people who had been expelled from Skender Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter is unable to hear the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: That's okay. That was the extent of the transcript that I wanted. Thank you, interpreters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After this initial speech, some names -- all of the names were read out. I won't play that for -- for time's sake today. What effect did reading the names out have on the family members?

utterances.speaker: SEIDA KARABASIC
utterances.text: It was particularly painful for them. As this lady read out names, mothers who heard their children's names read out fell to their knees. One man kept asking, "Where is my son? Why isn't he on this list? How come he's not on the list?" And as the lady kept reading out the list, mothers kept falling down, crying. This meant that this was the actual truth, that their children were gone, as their names had been on the list.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For the visit, I believe the organisation had purchased some flowers. Could you explain the purpose of the flowers on this day.

utterances.speaker: SEIDA KARABASIC
utterances.text: We bought 253 carnations in order to honour 253 residents of Prijedor who perished that day, and we gave the flowers to the families so that they could throw it down into the abyss, just as their children were pushed down into it. As they were throwing flowers, people leaned down above the abyss. One man who lost three brothers on that day threw down a carnation that fell on a branch down below but very near to the edge, and it seemed to me as if this man was ready to leap down, to follow the carnation. I grabbed him by the hand and I said, "Don't jump down there," and he said to me, "Maybe this is exactly what happened to my brother. Maybe he fell on a branch."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I know you recognise some of the people in the video. I'll just let it run for a moment, and then we'll stop it and I'll ask you to talk about some of the other stories.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please tell the Judges who the woman is hugging, the woman with the purple shirt.

utterances.speaker: SEIDA KARABASIC
utterances.text: The name of this woman is Fikra. Her daughter is hugging her. She's helping her to stay calm. She had lost her son and husband on that day, and she only had her daughter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There's a gentleman in this photo with a black shirt and a white vest. Can you identify him, please?

utterances.speaker: SEIDA KARABASIC
utterances.text: This is Hilmija Fazlic. He had lost a son on that day, on Vlasic. His son had been separated from the rest of the group. The son was -- the son's body was exhumed several days ago from a mass grave where there were a total of six bodies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As the crowd was walking away, what was the atmosphere like?

utterances.speaker: SEIDA KARABASIC
utterances.text: Many mothers and women needed to be assisted because they couldn't walk. We had to transport some in ambulances and we helped the others to get to the bus. One can see on this video that everybody's heads were hanging down. Everybody was very sad. And because they saw that something that they were hoping for was actually not realistic, that it was impossible that these people had survived, and they were having a very difficult time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When we spoke yesterday, you mentioned the rain that had started to fall at the end of the day. Could you tell the Judges what you told us.

utterances.speaker: SEIDA KARABASIC
utterances.text: When we got on the buses, as we were descending the Vlasic Mountain, it started raining. The clouds gathered. It rained heavily. And there was silence on the bus. People were saying that the rain represented tears, tears we are shedding because of our dearest ones who had perished on Vlasic on that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And lastly, given your extensive experience in dealing with the Koricani family members, I wanted to discuss some of the issues that are important to the families. First I believe you have told us that the families want the perpetrators brought to justice. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEIDA KARABASIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was very important for the families to have other perpetrators brought to justice for what they had done on that day. In addition to that, what is important for them is that all those who planned and ordered this crime to be committed be punished as well. What is most important for them is to find urgently the bodies of their family members so that they can be given a dignified burial.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Your Honour, no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Resch. Ms. Karabasic, in a court of law, an opportunity is also given to the Defence to put questions to you if there's any need to put questions to you. Is there any need, Mr. Dimitrijevic or Mr. Wachenheim, to --

utterances.speaker: MR. DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, we don't have questions

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since the Judges have also no questions for you, I'd like to thank you for having answered the questions put to you by the counsel for the Prosecution. And I would like to thank you for coming a very far way to The Hague and through your testimony make it possible for this Chamber to share your experience of the families of the victims which the Chamber deems of importance to hear in this case. Therefore, thank you very much for having come to The Hague, and you're excused. Madam Registrar, would you please --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I add something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you'd like to add something, please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to say on behalf of all the families that we are grateful to this Tribunal for everything it had done so far. We hope that the Tribunal will continue assisting the families in this way and that the Tribunal will punish all of the criminals for what they had done. And we hope that none of the pleas and plea bargaining would be at the detriment of the families, and we believe that everybody needs to be punished for what they had done. Somebody who killed 250 people cannot receive the same sentence as someone who killed one person. Therefore, a maximum sentence is in order. The families believe that you will follow this. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand what you just told us as expressing the feelings of those you have met, and I take it that you share those feelings. I can assure you that this Tribunal and everyone working in it will perform its task as good as they can. That's our task. And we have listened to your testimony, and it's part of what we will have to consider. Thank you very much for coming. Madam Registrar, would you then please escort the witness out of the courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The next issue on our agenda is a statement of Mr. Mrdja. I did understand, Mr. Mrdja, that you would primarily express your feelings to what happened and that you'll not enter into details as to what exactly happened. Because if you would give statements on facts in some detail, then it might be that we should ask you to make a solemn declaration as well. If, however, your statement is about your feelings and looking back to what happened, according to your guilty plea, then we could refrain from asking you to make a solemn declaration. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I will be very brief. Your Honours, thank you for giving me an opportunity at the end of this trial against me to address you with several words. In Yugoslavia, in a state where I was born, some 13 years ago a tragic conflict broke out. I was 20 years old at the time. Just like all people of my age, I desired peace and I had a number of plans for my future. The last thing on my mind was war and bloodshed. I knew about the war only what my parents told me, and they told me very little about the war. I didn't pay a lot of attention to that. At the time I believed war to be something from a distant past, something that happened way before I was born. Frankly speaking, until the very last moment I believed that I would be a member of a generation that would live its lifetime in peace. I grew up in a socialist system. At school I learned about brotherhood and unity between various peoples living in my country. However, I knew that a number of my ancestors perished in the previous war. I knew about the Jasenovac camp. However, at the time I was convinced that that was part of a distant past, something that did not concern me. I had peaceful relationships with my neighbours, Muslims and Croats. We lived together and socialised together, and I even had girlfriends that were non-Serbs. My parents never reproached me for that. In the beginning of the 1990s, things changed abruptly. Radio, television, press, everything was full of threats against Serbs and against Muslims, depending on whose media it was. Suddenly we started splitting along the lines of our thoughts and ideas at the time. It is difficult to comprehend it right now. Believing that we were faced with the same threat as Jasenovac was in the past, I responded to the mobilisation. I was young and strong, and exactly these kinds of people are needed in every army. I wanted to defend my people, and the last thing on my mind was attacking somebody else. In late spring 1992, I ended up in the intervention platoon of Prijedor Police. Terrible things were happening in Prijedor, and I would like to forget that. My neighbours and friends, Muslims, had to leave. As a policeman, before the 21st of August, I escorted and was -- provided security to several convoys leaving Prijedor. I cannot say that Muslims fared well there, but I know that most of them reached their destination safely. In the morning of the 21st of August, I was told that I had to escort another similar convoy. I didn't think that -- I apologise. I did not think that anything particular was going to happen. However, that's not how it was. At the order of the commander of the Intervention Platoon, who later was killed at the Bihac front - and I don't wish to mention his name now - we separated two bus loads of military-aged men. They were killed at Koricanske Stijene between Skender Vakuf and Travnik. I participated in separating and killing these innocent people. I have sincere remorse with respect to that, and I wish to offer my sincere apology to all the victims and their families. Your Honours, I hope that you will believe me. I did not commit this because I wanted to commit this or I enjoyed doing this. I did not hate these people. I did it because I was ordered to do so. My commander, who enjoyed great respect and had a lot of authority, was present personally and issued these orders. In those moments, I could not muster up enough courage to disobey the order. I can tell you now what would have happened had I refused to carry out the order; I assure you that they would have killed me right then. I hope that you believe me, Your Honours. All of my friends from the Intervention Platoon who could testify to this are afraid for their own future and they don't wish to testify. I cannot reproach them for this. Your Honours, in the past war, I was an ordinary rank and file soldier. I did not have a rank. I fought at many battlefronts and I behaved in a dignified manner. I faced many enemies and was wounded three times. And it is very difficult for me to face what happened at Koricanske Stijene. I asked to be transferred to another unit because I did not wish to kill innocent civilians. I spent the rest of my war service as a soldier who never committed anything similar to what had happened at Koricanske Stijene. This is the most difficult time of my past, and I would like to raise everything that had happened. However, I know it's not possible. I have in the meantime married and I have two children. I have lived after this in a dignified manner and have not committed any offences. I know that all of those families who lost their loved ones on the 21st of August, 1992 can see me only as a murderer and perhaps will think that my apologies are insincere. I can understand them for believing so, and I am prepared to serve time in order to pay for this. I hope that my confession will aid in ensuring that such things are never repeated in our territory. I know that by doing so I can help in some way remove some of the burden that I've been carrying for 11 years; however, I know that this will stay with me until the day I die. Once again, I offer my sincere apology to all of the families, and I thank you, Your Honours, for allowing me to address you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mrdja, please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, until 5.30 we would have approximately three-quarters of an hour. That's also the time that has been scheduled for closing arguments by the Prosecution. Would you be able to finish in approximately three-quarters of an hour?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I believe so, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may we begin, however, by moving briefly into private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are in open session again. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.
