Mr. President, Your Honours, learned colleagues for the Defence, we are here today to consider the imposition of an appropriate sentence for the commission of a crime that stands out even against the backdrop of widespread persecution, destruction, and murder in 1992. Indeed, no matter how quickly that crime is summarised, its chilling nature is manifest. On August 21st, 1992, Bosnian Serb authorities organised a convoy of trucks and buses to remove Muslims from Prijedor to Muslim-held territory in Travnik. Many of the passengers had recently been released from the brutal camps of Omarska and Keraterm. Members of the Prijedor Police Intervention Squad, as you have heard, including the accused, controlled the convoy. En route, they robbed the passengers of their last possessions. Shortly before the convoy reached its intended destination, indeed within a few kilometres of refuge, the policemen escorting the convoy separated in excess of 200 military-age men from the others, men who were then crammed onto two buses and driven to the location at Koricanske Stijene. As the Court has now seen, it is a site that symbolises the utter perversity of war, a location of extraordinary natural beauty that became a mass grave. Acting upon orders from their superiors, the Intervention Squad members removed the men from the buses, in groups of various sizes lined them up, and murdered them one after another. The bodies of the dead or dying which did not fall immediately into the abyss were pushed into the ravine. Although the Intervention Squad attempted to finish off any survivors with grenades or gunfire, as you have heard and as you have seen here today, miraculously a handful survived. Now, on the basis of what we have heard from one of those survivors, from a representative of family members, indeed from the accused himself, from the documentary evidence previously submitted concerning the crime, this Court must now determine the appropriate sentence. In so doing, you will be guided by a number of factors that the parties have addressed in their sentencing briefs. I should note that the briefs reveal no significant dispute insofar as I can determine about the most important factor to be considered in sentencing, the gravity of the crime, nor about the two other critical factors affecting this proceeding, the entry of a plea of guilty and the cooperation of the accused. Before addressing those issues, however, I would like to discuss the matters about which there is some dispute. Now, a number of these are relatively minor and I believe would only have a negligible impact upon the sentence irrespective of how they were resolved. However, they are matters potentially affecting the jurisprudence of the Tribunal and, therefore, merit comment. It's a lengthy list. I will run through it very quickly and then assure the Court that my discussion of those issues will be as concise as possible. Those matters include the following: The weight to be given a crime against humanity in comparison to other crimes; age as a mitigating or aggravating factor in this case; remorse; the effect of the length of time between the commission of an offence and judgement; the effect of incarceration in a foreign country; the issue of the vulnerability of victims; the accused's position as a policeman as it may affect sentencing; the issue of credit for the accused's conduct while in custody or the cooperation of the Defence with the Chamber during the pendency of the case; the timing of the entry of guilty plea; the psychiatrist -- or excuse me, the psychologist's report; the issue of duress and orders; and finally the application of the law of Bosnia and Herzegovina insofar as sentencing is concerned. I appreciate this is a long list, Your Honour, and as I indicated, I will be as concise as possible in dealing with the issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If -- perhaps you and also the Defence would keep in mind that the Judges have all carefully read what is in the sentencing briefs. So whatever has to be added or has to be given more nuance, of course we'd like to a listen to that, but it's not necessary to repeat anything that is in the sentencing briefs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Yes. And I have been guided by discussions with Defence counsel concerning their submissions - as you know, the briefs were submitted at the same time - and also by a brief 65 ter. First, with respect to the first issue, I would note that the Prosecution does not assert that Count 3, which is charged as a crime against humanity, should be given greater weight than Count 2, which is a violation of the laws and customs of war. Both counts arise from the same facts and should be assessed accordingly. I would also note that this general issue was of course resolved by the Tadic Appeals Chamber, which held that "After full consideration, the Appeals Chamber takes the view that there is in law no distinction between the seriousness of a crime against humanity and that of a war crime." I would only note that, to the extent that any element of either crime to which the accused pled guilty may be significant to the Court - for example, the existence of a widespread or systematic attack - the Court may consider it in its deliberations, but again, we are not urging the Court to bifurcate the counts as if they came from separate incidents. With respect to age has a mitigating factor, or aggravating factor in a case of victim, although age can be either a mitigating factor in the case of an accused or an aggravating factor based on the age of the victim, the Prosecution does not assert that age should be invoked as either a mitigating or aggravating factor in this case, notwithstanding any suggestion to the contrary in the written submission. Next, remorse. Let me note the following points about the issue of remorse: First of all, it is a potential factor in mitigation that is independent of a plea of guilty, independent of acceptance of responsibility, and independent of cooperation, although clearly there may be some overlap in the analysis. But I say that because the result is that remorse must consist of something more than any one of those separate and independent factors. Secondly, I would note that remorse refers to a state of mind and as such is relatively unique among the factors in mitigation, because of its subjectivity. And in order to guard against its reduction to a form of a meaningless incantation by an accused, the Chamber must consider the existence of objective circumstances reflecting that state of mind. Now, here the accused asserts that the conduct, the objective conduct reflecting remorse, can be found in his request for reassignment from the Intervention Squad shortly after the massacre at Koricanske Stijene.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you a question in this respect, and perhaps also address the Defence at the same time. I think in the sentencing brief it's also the Defence has said that the accused has asked to be transferred to another unit, and reference is at that very moment made to Annex -- let me just try to find it. I think it was Annex -- I'm just looking for the right footnote. He requested to be transferred -- look at page 13 of the English version. And in footnote 50 you refer to the certificate of the Ministry of Defence, Department of Prijedor. I have, just as a matter of factual basis of -- of the argument which I find in the sentencing brief and which is addressed by the Prosecution, could you indicate to me where exactly that document says that he asked to be transferred rather than that he served at a different ... Perhaps meanwhile you could also solve another problem I noticed. That is, that following -- let me just see. In this document, I have some difficulties to -- to reconcile the original version of the translation. Perhaps you could look at it. It's pages -- the ones that have been filed, it was page -- Annex A, number 8, pages 785 and 786. I have some difficulties, first of all, to find where the document says that he -- he himself asked to be -- be transferred to another unit. And the second problem is that 785 doesn't look very much as an original of what is presented as translation in 786. It just gives you one clue -- one document says that -- the one you referred to, the English version, is a document of the 29th of July, 2002; whereas, the original seems to be a document of 16th of April of 2003. And also for other reasons it's not easy to reconcile one document being the translation of the other. Could you please first -- because that's the factual basis of the issue Mr. Tieger addresses at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm afraid that I steal time from Mr. Tieger, but I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will compensate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Maybe it is not -- you misunderstood what -- what we said. We didn't say that there was some official request and in this time it wasn't possible, but we only put the evidence from which it is visible that he changed the unit in that exact time, and that is the 9th of September from 1992. But official request, there was not. In addition to this claim, we have also other evidence, but I am afraid that we have to go to private session again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If necessary, we will do so. Perhaps you -- but then perhaps the other question, whether 785 is the original of what, of an English text we find in 786.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Also, Your Honour, frankly I don't have any kind of translation. There is only the English version of sentencing brief. I never -- I never sent anything in -- but translation of documents, that's another issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you are referring in your sentencing brief to the document which bears the number as I see it on 786, which is without any doubt a translation. It's at least an English text. And all the annexes to the sentencing briefs, I always find first the English and then what appears to be the original, apart from on pages 786, where I see an English text, which seems not to be the translation of the next page, which is 785. And if it's not a translation of 785, I cannot understand 785, because I've got no translation. I think that both documents deal with a similar matter, since it seems that similar dates appear in both documents, but one is certainly not a translation of the other. Perhaps you take your time during the break in order to clarify this issue and --

utterances.speaker: MR. DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you'd need to know exactly what it is, I could -- have you found them?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I know what you need.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: And I will try.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then, Mr. Tieger, although it has not been fully clarified, please proceed. Or do you first want to go into private session to further explain? Okay. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour, that was one of the points I wanted to raise with the Court about its own efforts to assess the weight to be given the objective circumstances cited by the Defence in support of the distance of remorse. I would also note a couple of other factors that may be of benefit to the Court in making that assessment. One other factor is that the members of the Intervention Squad were all dispatched from Prijedor shortly after the incident as part of the cover-up of the crime. Another factor which may cut in the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I again ask, in order to avoid whatever confusion, I take it that you are - let me just find my notes - that you are referring to material in support of the indictment, a letter of Mr. Simo Drljaca in which he explains that on from the 9th of September, 1992 all police officers that were involved -- is that the source?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dimitrijevic, that's also something that came into my mind. Just in order to assist you, that would be page 33 of the material supporting the indictment. That's a letter from Mr. Simo Drljaca which reads - I'll just confront you with it - "We are unable to investigate the alleged killing of a number of people of Muslim nationality in the area of Koricanske Stijene because all the policemen who escorted the convoy to Travnik - and then it's unclear whether it says the 21st of August - have been in the battlefield of Hasan Pijesak since 9 September 1992." I take it you were aware of the existence of this disclosed document, and the emphasis on the request to be transferred briefly after the event at Koricanske Stijene does not address in whatever way the existence of at least one document which seems to indicate that all police officers on from the 9th of September were far away from the area of Prijedor and were now in Han Pijesak so that therefore the -- I would say the exclusivity of the step taken by Mr. Mrdja, apart from whether it was his step - because that's not documented by this -- by this -- by the annexes - whether that would need any further comment, because the Chamber has to decide on the basis of probability. It's -- you invoke it as a mitigating circumstance. So I wonder how in your view we would have to deal with your submissions at this moment compared to what has been presented in support of the indictment when confirmation was sought and which material is known to you, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour. It's clear that Darko Mrdja was on the battlefield in Han Pijesak. And after the 21st of August, I think the 24th of August that he went to Han Pijesak with all other police officers from the Intervention Squad and that is not in dispute. But he was wounded on that -- on that battlefield, and he went back to Prijedor, and after that he made a request to go to military unit. I didn't really know that this you will find as some kind of collision that document signed by Simo Drljaca, and the document signed in Ministry of Defence, because I don't see any -- any dispute between those two documents. But now I am in a position only what I can call Mr. Mrdja to testify about that event that he was -- that he was wounded in the -- that he was as other members of Prijedor Intervention Squad, he was on the battlefield in Han Pijesak, he returned back home because he was wounded, and after that he -- he asked to be transferred to another military unit. That's -- that's how we reconcile all of these things what you put on the table right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think there's no contradiction. But we understood your argument to be that briefly after the event happened, that Mr. Mrdja had applied for being transferred to another unit, and that's the dates we find on both of this, both the original and the translation of that document, and it -- it gave the impression - let me express myself carefully - that this was a specific -- a specific request made by Mr. Mrdja. But I now do understand that there's no misunderstanding - at least, that's what you just told me - that on the 9th of September - which is two weeks after the event. And we find the 9th of September also in the translation and also in the original of which I do not know exactly what it is - that all police officers involved in this incident were at Han Pijesak.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, and that was the response of Simo Drljaca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yeah. And I thought you said that you didn't dispute that. But let me just check that. He went to Han Pijesak with all other police officers from the Intervention Squad. That's what you said, according to the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I said that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: That is exactly what I said. But we are talking now about 9th September.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly. And when he went to Han Pijesak, it wasn't 9th September; it was a few days after the 21st of August. That's -- and we consider also 9th September as something that is very close to 21st of August. It's not -- that's how we consider that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Please proceed. I'm trying to clarify factual basis for your argument now and then. And of course, I'll take into consideration that this interrupts the -- your argument. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: On that same subject, Your Honour, just a couple of additional points that may be of benefit to the Court in making its assessment. And I think they may be considered as countervailing points, but I believe I need to bring them to the Court's attention. One is the fact that insofar as we can determine the accused, unlike at least some of the other perpetrators, did not return to the Prijedor Police after Han Pijesak. The other factor, I note from the jurisprudence, is that Chambers have traditionally considered the statement of the accused in court, both to -- as an opportunity to assess interpersonally the apparent contrition and also, I think, as an objective contribution to the extent a public expression of remorse can be. So I offer that to the -- to the Court for its use in assessing this factor. I move now to the Defence submission that the length of time between the criminal conduct and the judgement is a factor in mitigation in this particular case. The Defence cites three sources; a United States supreme court case, a 1931 commentary, and German law. The US Supreme Court case, we submit, is entirely unhelpful in the analysis here because it addresses a case in which the Prosecution affirmatively sought procedural advantage by repeatedly requesting delays in the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're now referring to Barker versus Wingo?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The commentary, we also submit, is similarly unhelpful because it concerns itself with the adverse impact on prosecutive objectives of a delay, and it suggests that prosecutive goals and objectives are undermined by a delay in the process. Now, whether that's true or not, it is surely not a factor that accrues to the mitigation of an accused's sentence. So I turn now to the German law, which does appear to take the position that the passage of time between the criminal conduct and the judgement may be a factor in mitigation of sentence. The -- the only rationale cited by the Defence, however, and the only rationale we were able to find in the materials available to us, looking at the case cited by the Defence, is that delay can be an important mitigating factor because the State's need to punish diminishes over time. And insofar as can be gleaned from the Defence brief, that means that essentially that the risk to society from an individual perpetrator diminishes over time, particularly if that perpetrator, while passing the time from the criminal conduct has not engaged in further criminal conduct. That rationale, I think, has limited utility here. The deterrent impact of Prosecution -- excuse me, of Tribunal prosecutions and sentences is not limited or even primarily focused on the individual perpetrator because, for the most part, the circumstances that gave rise to the criminal conduct are -- cannot reasonably be expected to recur for that particular individual. Instead, the deterrent effect of -- and the deterrent objective of prosecution -- of Tribunal sentencing is aimed at those elsewhere who may find themselves in a similar position and by imposing sentence in an international setting, the Tribunal intends to say that such conduct will not be tolerated and it will receive appropriate punishment. That objective, the Prosecution submits, is not diminished over time and the rationale that appears in the German domestic cases is not useful or strongly applicable here. If I may, let me turn to the question of incarceration in a foreign country, which the Defence also cites as a factor in mitigation. They contend that serving time in a foreign country constitutes a particular hardship that should be reflected in a reduced sentence for two reasons: First, because the accused would not speak the language of the country of incarceration; and second, because he would not receive visits from family and friends. We have noted that the only authority cited in support of that proposition is a German case, a case which itself asserts that language difficulties, the first reason in support of that case, are of reduced significance if a long-term prison sentence is imposed or anticipated; the kinds of sentences we deal with here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I again interrupt you, Mr. Tieger, because I'm trying to follow your argument. I take it that you are referring to the case referred to in footnote 66. But I would first like to ask the Defence: It gives as the source BGH St, which stands for criminal law. Should I address you? Yes. But on number 43 -- number 23 is a case about the costs of the Defence; on the other hand, on page 234 -- well, as a matter of fact, on page 233, there appears a case which is published under number 35, which appears to be the one you're referring to. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. WACHENHEIM
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are talking about the impact that serving a sentence in a foreign country has?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WACHENHEIM
utterances.text: Okay. May I just check, because I have the commentary with me and there might have been a mistake in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's first check whether we're all talking about the same case, because the reference is not clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. WACHENHEIM
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm still looking for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Well, perhaps, Mr. Tieger, you will continue, and then we'll take it that we are referring to 43, number 35, instead of 23; although, it would save a lot of time, I can promise you, if the quotations are correct. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. So our first point is that when long-term confinement is anticipated, the language problem is relatively quickly resolved and over the long term has a relatively negligible impact, according to the very case cited by the Defence. Secondly, we have noted the following: That the cases cited by the Defence assert explicitly that it is -- that confinement in a foreign country is not sufficient in and of itself to show a particular hardship or to demonstrate that the accused or defendant in that case will suffer a particular hardship. Instead, the German case law cited appears to hold it depends on the particular circumstances and personal circumstances of the accused. Absent a particularised showing of the hardship that would result from such confinement, according to the cases cited by the Defence, there is no basis for a claim in mitigation. If -- if generalised suggestions about confinement, rather than specifics, are sufficient, then the Prosecution would -- would note that the countries that have agreed to accept convicted accused from this Tribunal are known to be among those of the most progressive penal systems in the world, and therefore we would submit relatively beneficial circumstances could be anticipated, rather than hardship. Now, this may or may not turn out to be specifically true, but it is as reasonable a generality, we submit, as one that the Defence offers. Absent a particularised showing, there's no basis for such a claim in mitigation. And finally, we would note that every accused in this institution will serve time in a foreign country and that -- that factor is intrinsic to and already subsumed by the Tribunal's existing sentencing practice. Your Honour, before turning to the next issue, this may be an appropriate time for a break, but I would certainly leave it to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hesitate to ask you, because I've interrupted you several times. How much time would you still need, Mr. Tieger, do you think?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I would imagine approximately 15 to 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 15 to 20 minutes. I'm afraid that that would not do with the tapes, and also the interpreters might get tired. If you could find a suitable moment, either here or within the next five minutes, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This is fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then we'll adjourn. Let's -- since we'd like to finish by 7.00, let's see whether we couldn't start at ten minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, please proceed. I expect you to finish shortly after five past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The Prosecution in its sentencing brief asserted that the Kvocka case supports the proposition that committing crimes while in the position of a police officer is an aggravating factor. The Defence has taken the position that the Kvocka judgement actually turns on other facts. We have reviewed the judgement again and take heed of the Defence position that it is not precisely on point because of the different factors emphasised in that case. In that case, the Chamber focused on the impact that the three accused who were -- positions were found to have aggravated the crime, had on other guards in the institution. Nevertheless, we feel we must emphasise the heightened powers and responsibilities that attach to the police -- position of policeman and we would point the Chamber to United States sentencing guideline jurisprudence for an example of a national jurisdiction where the position of police officer may be seen as an aggravating factor. With respect to vulnerable victims, also a factor cited by the Prosecution as an aggravating factor. The Defence position, as we understand it, is the Plavsic case has held that it is not an independent factor but is instead subsumed under the overall gravity of the offence. It should first be noted in that respect that the Plavsic sentencing Chamber explicitly stated that the vulnerability of the victims is indeed capable of amounting to an aggravating factor. In that case, however, it was held to be subsumed within the overall gravity of the offence and basically considered under that particular rubric. Now, in some sentencing systems, where there is a quantifiable value attached to a sentencing factor, then the question of where that circumstance falls and under which factor it's assessed, whether the overall gravity of the offence or under a specific sentencing -- a specific aggravating factor can have a quantifiable impact on the sentence. But in a system such as ours, where the question is whether or not the Court should assess that as a significant factor, I think it is of little moment whether it falls under the overall gravity of the offence or whether it's looked as a potential "aggravating factor" so long as the Court considers it and assesses it with its proper weight and accords it a proper evaluation, and that's what we seek here. Very quickly with respect to behaviour and good conduct while in custody or the issue of counsel's cooperation with the Court, we recognise they have been cited in various cases. It's our position, however, that those are not factors which were intended to fall within the meaning of mitigated sentences. In the first place, accused persons receive credit for appropriate behaviour while in custody, both in the form of appropriate privileges and ultimately in the form of good-time credits; and with respect to cooperation with the Court, we feel that that's an obligation of the lawyers as officers of the court and one which is not intended to be invoked as a mitigating factor. A question has been raised about the timing of the entry of the plea, and the Defence has asserted that a plea would have been entered at an even earlier stage had it -- had discussions with the Prosecution proceeded in a different way and had the -- more specifically, had the indictment been framed in a different manner. I note, first of all, that I don't think there's been any suggestion that the Defence should receive less credit because of the timing of the plea. So I'm not sure how much weight they seek to be attached to that factor. But irrespective of how much weight they seek, I don't think the record supports the invocation of that circumstance as a mitigating factor. As it stands, the record shows little more than fruitless discussions between the parties. In addition, the assertion that the language -- the factual allegation language of the indictment was the only factor standing between the plea of not guilty and a plea of guilty, I think is contradicted by the fact that the plea agreement itself contained more factors than that and -- and obviously the resolution of the case through a guilty plea required more discussion than simply about the factual language of the indictment. There's been some discussion about -- some allusion, at any rate, to duress, and we really think we should -- any evaluation of that issue must begin with the distinction between duress and the issue of following orders. Duress within our jurisprudence means imminent threats to the life of an accused if he refuses to commit a crime. And obviously doesn't refer to the more commonplace and everyday use of the term. It is our position that the facts as asserted by the Defence do not support duress within the meaning of the Tribunal's jurisdiction. We would point the Court to the Erdemovic case and cite the contrast between the circumstances of those two cases. In the Erdemovic case, the accused refused the order and then was expressly told that if he did not comply he would be killed. That is not the scenario that unfolded here. The suggestion that such a risk nevertheless existed is clearly more speculative than the circumstance cited and relied upon in Erdemovic. And furthermore, it should be evaluated at least in the context of the accused's asserted request to leave the Intervention Squad based on the events at Koricanske Stijene. But I cited the distinction between "duress" and "following orders," and that should be pursued. Article 7(4) of the Statute of the Tribunal provides that the fact that an accused person acted pursuant to an order of a government or a superior may be considered in mitigation of punishment. Now, the Prosecution accepts that the accused was acting under orders. As a general matter, we note that the mere fact of receiving an order does not necessarily reduce an accused's culpability for a crime. One can readily imagine a circumstance where a superior gives an order to a subordinate who is as fully committed to the objective as the superior and the -- a fulfilment of the order indicates no more than the realisation of a mutually desired objective. Here, however, we accept that the accused had good relations with his Muslim neighbours before the conflict, and we -- more importantly, we accept that his involvement in the Intervention Squad and in the crimes to which he pled guilty reflected his acceptance of the authority of the Bosnian Serb leadership from top to bottom and the goals and the rationales they espoused. And to the extent that the mitigating impact, the mitigating effect of 7(4) reflects the distinction that must be made between leaders and the person they use as tools to implement their illegal objectives, then this factor is relevant here for the Court's consideration. I will only turn briefly to the psychiatrist's report. I'm not going to question Dr. Gallwitz's expertise, but perhaps for reasons beyond his control, I think the report is superficial and betrays a lack of understanding of the circumstances of the conflict or of the offence. And I will only add that -- that the -- the focus of the report on the distinction between a kind of platonic ideal state in which a wholly independent judgement can be made, a sort of glass-bubble scenario, is contrasted with the number of factors or number of influences including age, indoctrination, the brutality of war, obedience, all of which, I submit, are essentially -- or essentially represent a litany of the circumstances of war applying to everyone involved in that conflict. Finally, with respect to the factors I wanted to enumerate and then I will address the other fact, the other two factors I mentioned, that's the application of BiH law, of Bosnian law. As I understand the Defence submission, they are suggesting the following: That there were two kinds of penalties available in Bosnia in 1992; one up to a period of 15 years, the other in Article 38 provided that the Court could impose a sentence of imprisonment for a term of 20 years for criminal acts eligible for the death penalty. It's the Defence's position that once the death penalty was abolished, it therefore left no hook for that provision. And because, in their view, a term of 20 years could only be imposed for criminal acts eligible for the death penalty, then the sentencing law reverted to the more lenient 15-year provision. Now, we submit that that would clearly reflect a kind of anomaly in the law and an odd technicality in violation of the spirit of the law, which indicates that there's a death penalty but the Court could also impose 20 years. One would find it odd that the abolition of the death penalty would similarly be intended to undercut the -- the penalty -- the non-death penalty provision of that same law. And, in fact, that rational approach to legislation is indeed found in the law, we submit. The Defence cited Article 38. They did not cite Article 37, which provides that the death penalty may not be imposed as the only principal punishment for a certain criminal act. And that was in effect at the same time that Article 38 came into effect. It's our submission that Article 37 reflects the rational spirit, rational interpretation of the law, that is, that these are alternative personalities, that for the gravest crimes the Court could impose a sentence of either 20 years or the death penalty. The abolition of the death penalty simply meant that now the Court could only impose the 20 years. That's our submission with respect to BiH law. Your Honour, it's my responsibility at this point, I think to address the principal factors affecting the determination of sentence in the case; the gravity of the offence on the one hand and the acceptance of responsibility through a guilty plea and cooperation on the other. In our sentencing brief, we have cited the applicable case law in this institution regarding the significance of the gravity of the offence. I will only state that the -- that Chambers have over and over reaffirmed the principal that it is the gravity of the offence, it is the primary consideration in the imposition of sentence. And we have also highlighted for the Court in our sentencing brief the factors which the Court must consider in making that assessment, essentially including the individual circumstances of the crime, as it was stated in the Krstic case. This presupposes taking into account quantitatively the number of victims and qualitatively the suffering inflicted on the victims. The gravity of this crime, Your Honour, is perhaps best exemplified by the sheer impossibility of doing that which I know every member of this Chamber would seek to do, and that is consider individually the victims. This impossible task, we submit, reveals perhaps more clearly than anything else the magnitude of this crime. Nevertheless, in making that effort, we urge this Chamber, as we indicate in our brief, to consider the despair of those who were torn from their loved ones a short distance from safety, the terror of those who -- who waited while their comrades fell, and the agony of those who did not perish immediately but died in -- died slowly of their injuries and of exposure. And of course, the Court must also consider those who survived and the indirect victims, the families. I then turn to the accused's entry of plea and his cooperation. I will won't go beyond the details already provided to the Chamber earlier, and I will leave any more detailed submissions to the Defence. It's my obligation, however, to observe, for the benefit of this Chamber, that this is a factor of considerable importance and that the accused has substantially and meaningfully cooperated in a manner that merits substantial consideration. Your Honours, we have attempted to assess and to balance all of the factors that are relevant to sentence and that affect the imposition of sentence here, and we've done that in full recognition of the fact that there is no single sentence that can fully satisfy all of the sometimes competing considerations that apply to sentencing in any given case. On the one hand here, even the maximum sentence cannot fully capture the gravity of the crime. And on the other hand, crimes against too many other victims will go completely unredressed unless this institution is able to deploy its resources in the most efficient and most effective manner, including securing the cooperation of insider witnesses. In addition, I should note, as a recent editorial observed about information from insider witnesses and from perpetrators, that information provides a truth that the international community and history could otherwise not have acquired. So in this case, the Prosecution has considered what has been accomplished by this plea of guilty and acceptance of responsibility, and it includes some of the following factors: One of the most significant crimes of this conflict can no longer be denied or simply dismissed as the responsibility of a few madmen. This crime was committed pursuant to orders, orders of the authorities, and that fact, Your Honours, must be incorporated into an understanding of the conflict of anyone in the region who has the courage to inquire. I think we know that in a country where the only hope for the future is that its people can live together, the first step, the fundamental step, is an acknowledgment of the suffering and the crimes of the past. I think it's fair to say that the accused's acceptance of responsibility and his cooperation have struck a blow against a long-standing wall of denial, a wall that must eventually either fall or that will forever block the path to the future. Your Honours, for all of the reasons I've cited and for those which appear in our sentencing brief, the Prosecution respectfully reaffirms its recommendation that a sentence be imposed in the range of 15 to 20 years. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. Before I give the opportunity to the Defence for their closing arguments, may I just ask you. There's one issue; you relied several times on the impact of the -- of these events on the families. There is, however, jurisprudence in this Tribunal in the case of the Prosecutor versus Krnojelac where it is specifically said that such effects - that's effects not on the victims themselves but on the family members - are irrelevant to the culpability of the offender and that it would be unfair to consider such effects in determining sentence. Have you thought about that or will you give it some thought when the Defence gives its closing argument? Have you considered that there is at least one decision in this Tribunal that would oppose against taking into consideration what you said we should take into consideration?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- thank you for the opportunity to address that. I will tell you candidly that that matter is one that was not fully briefed. I would welcome the opportunity, because I think it is a significant issue, to respond to the Court, the Court's inquiry in a more fulsome way. I could certainly offer the Court our position on it and our reaction to Krnojelac. But if the Court would permit, I would ask for the -- for permission to submit a more reasoned and well-researched response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand that I've surprised you a bit with it. Let's see, on the other hand, there's also a major interest to be served by finishing by today, so let's -- you could at least give it some thought --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- whether you would agree with this case or not. Mr. Dimitrijevic, is it you who is going to give the closing argument of the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: -- Your Honour. Before I start with my closing arguments, you put me, Your Honour, one question regarding the documents in the sentencing brief --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: -- attached to the sentencing brief. And I looked at that. I don't know why, but page 786 is the English version of document under the page 789. And I didn't find page 785, because we didn't put those page numbers. That's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: So that's basically -- if you will allow me, I will proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Honourable Judges, learned colleagues from the Office of the Prosecutor, this Tribunal was established in 1993, in the middle of the war that took place in Bosnia and Herzegovina as a response by the international community to the massive violences of humanitarian law in the former Yugoslavia and particularly Bosnia and Herzegovina. The main goal --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Defence counsel please slow down a little for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Effective measures --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you to slow down a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And at the same time ask, perhaps, Mr. Wachenheim to check the numbers. I'll give you what is 789 in my file. I'll give you what is 785 in my file, which looks very much as if it would be 789, because 5 and 9 are easily to be -- if you could please return it to me later. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: In resolution number 808, dated the 22nd February, 1993, the Security Council of the United Nations, inter alia said: "Expressing once again its grave alarm at continuing reports of widespread violations of international humanitarian law occurring within the territory of the former Yugoslavia, including reports of mass killings and the continuance of practice of `ethnic cleansing'." We think that one of the events that gave rise to this attitude of alarm by the Security Council and caused it to establish this Tribunal was the Mount Vlasic massacre in Bosnia-Herzegovina on 21st August, 1992. On that day, a convoy was organised by authorities in Prijedor. Almost 2.000 non-Serbs were transported to Travnik, a town that was under the control of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which was loyal to the government in Sarajevo. However, two buses from this convoy, loaded with military-aged men, unfortunately never reached their destination. They were less than 10 kilometres from the front line that divided the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and from the Army of Republika Srpska when they were separated from the rest of convoy. While the rest of the convoy continued its journey to Travnik, members of the Intervention Squad, among them Darko Mrdja, took the two bus loads of men to a place nearby known as Koricanske Stijene, where they executed them. The number of dead will probably never be accurately established. Estimates are that between 160 and 228 men were executed. Every human life is unique and unrepeatable. Human lives cannot be treated as mere numbers. That is why the Defence from the very beginning did not insist on establishing of accurate number of murdered victims, because from our point of view it is not realistic that this number will be ever reached. Out of any dispute is that this massacre happened and that a large number of people were killed. By a miracle, 12 men survived. We had an opportunity to hear one of them, Midhet Mujkanovic at this sentence hearing. Any comments about this emotional testimony is superfluous. The Defence does not want to deal with the history of the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, where transformation from victim to perpetrator have repeatedly taken place throughout history during the periods between wars. Respectfully, this Trial Chamber had a lot of opportunities, through other cases, and on the basis of its own studying to learn a lot about history, not only Bosnia and Herzegovina but the whole former Yugoslavia. Bearing in mind its responsibilities, the Defence wants to draw the attention of this Honourable Trial Chamber to facts that are, from our point of view, relevant for sentencing in this case. And we shall take this opportunity and examine the points that we -- that were raised by our learned colleagues from the Office of the Prosecutor. Article 24, paragraph 2 of the Statute is a starting point in sentencing. It directs, inter alia, that Trial Chambers should take into account the gravity of the crime and individual circumstances connected with the accused. To apply this article correctly, as the condition sine qua non, this Honourable Chamber must take into account the circumstances of Darko Mrdja. This is logical, because otherwise all who had participated in any form in this crime will liable -- will be liable for a crime with the same gravity. Both crimes that Darko Mrdja is accused originate from the same event; murder, a violence of the laws and customs of war, punishable under Article 3 of the Statute that related to the murder of a large number of men, estimated in excess of 200, and inhuman acts (attempted murder), as a crime against humanity, punishable under Article 5 of the Statute, related to 12 survivors of same event. Darko Mrdja pled guilty on both counts and he was informed about differences between those two crimes. However, following such indictments -- indictment, the Defence concludes that in a situation wherein no one survived, Darko Mrdja would be accused only for one count, murder, a violation of the laws and customs of war, punishable under Article 3 of the Statute. That is why the Defence considers that a crime against humanity, punishable under Article 5 of the Statute (attempted murder), although being grave, in the present case does not bear any additional weight of its own. This does not mean that Darko Mrdja or his Defence contests in any way the existence of conditions necessary to apply Article 5 of the Statute. The Defence welcomes the attitude of the OTP, given in paragraph 16 of their sentencing brief that Darko Mrdja was not an architect of the massacre but only one of those who implemented the orders of his superiors. This is consistent with the factual basis of the plea agreement. If you do not take into account these personal circumstances, then those who planned and ordered the crimes would be punished the same as those who implemented the orders. We do not put in any way in question criminal liability of the perpetrators of this crime. Such criminal liability extends to Darko Mrdja as well, and he pleaded guilty in this court. However, something what we want to draw special attention to is the role of Darko Mrdja in this event. We find it necessary to emphasise this, especially due to the fact that as far as we know there is no pending procedure in this Tribunal or in any national court against any of the co-perpetrators or direct superiors. Truthfully, in other Tribunal cases the massacre on Koricanske Stijene has been mentioned but in a heap of other accusations it is lost from sight. Bearing this in mind, the Defence fears that Darko Mrdja's individual circumstances will also be lost. Justification of this fear arises from the title of this case on the ICTY web site. This case has a name "Vlasic Mountain." Such title is only partly accurate. This criminal procedure against Darko Mrdja is most likely only the first part of a procedure that will have a subject Vlasic Mountain massacre. The Defence and Darko Mrdja do not want to minimise his liability as one of the perpetrators, but without -- without his participation and participation of other members of Intervention Squad together, no illegal order would have been executed. However, the Defence insists that individual circumstances are part of the gravity of the crime, because without that there is not individualisation of the guilt. Instead, we are entering the field of objective criminal liability. At this point we would like to draw your attention to what we think to one error in the Prosecution sentencing brief. In paragraph 7 of this brief, the OTP cites the Krstic judgement and quotes the part of paragraph 698, and quotes: "The seriousness of the crime must weigh heavily in the sentence imposed irrespective of the criminal participation of the individual." However, text of the same paragraph that Defence has says: "The seriousness of the crime must weigh heavily in the sentence imposed irrespective of the form of the criminal participation of the individual." So the OTP dropped from the original words "of the form." We do not consider this error as intentional; however, it is our responsibility to notice it because the sentence has an entirely different meaning. So the Defence considers that crimes that are Darko Mrdja accused are serious breaches of international humanitarian and war law; otherwise, there would not be a jurisdiction in this Honourable Tribunal. However, when assessing the gravity of these crimes, we cannot solely rely upon the number of victims but must consider the individual circumstances of Darko Mrdja as well. The Defence in its sentencing brief argues that there are no aggravating circumstances in this case. After consideration of the arguments made by OTP in its sentencing brief and today, at this hearing we remain at the same position, that there are no aggravating circumstances. The OTP considers that vulnerability of the victims is an aggravating factor on the side of Darko Mrdja. With all respect, Defence disagrees. Both of the crimes for which Darko Mrdja have pled guilty have quantitative element defining the status of the victims as a prerequisite of the crimes. Just this attribute of victims was one of the reasons for defining this crime separately from classical criminal law under national laws. In other words, when we deal with the classical criminal offence of murder, under whatever national legislation we can conceive various degrees of vulnerability of victims and some national legislation foresee so-called qualified form of murder. As far as the crimes encompassed by the jurisdiction of this Honourable Tribunal are concerned, because those crimes involve international humanitarian law, they necessarily include vulnerable victims. It seems that the arguments of the OTP in this respect cannot suffer serious criticism. This is especially concerning the arguments that the victims were unarmed and perpetrators heavily armed, that victims were stripped of their rights, refugees in their own country, et cetera. As an argumentum a contrario, we raise the question of whether those crimes can be committed against somebody who is armed, whose rights are being respected, and who is protected by the state. Truthfully, such a position was taken by the Trial Chamber in the Aleksovski case. However, with all due respect, very weak arguments are given to support it. It is said that national legislation foresees situations when handicapped persons are victims. The Defence considers this are -- this is classical -- classic criminal law that we have discussed earlier in reference to particularly qualified forms. On the other side, crimes coming within the Tribunal's jurisdiction are per se qualified and the vulnerability of the victims is subsumed in their gravity. This position was taken by the Trial Chamber in the Biljana Plavsic case, when in paragraph 58 of the sentencing judgement from 23rd February 2003 it refused to consider the vulnerability of victims as an aggravating circumstance. It is also the same position taken by the Trial Chamber in the Drazen Erdemovic sentencing judgement because the vulnerability of victims in this case was not considered as an aggravating factor. The second aggravating factor mentioned in the Prosecutor's sentencing brief is Darko Mrdja's so-called position of authority. The Defence considers that relying in this respect on Kvocka and other judgements is not adequate. To the contrary, from this judgement, one can easily conclude that Darko Mrdja had no position of authority as an aggravating factor. Namely, it is not in dispute that Darko Mrdja had been --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: -- had been mobilised as a policeman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you to slow down. The interpreters have difficulties in following you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Okay. And that he did not receive almost any police training. Unlike Kvocka, Prcac and Radic, he was not a professional policeman. Instead, Darko Mrdja's situation was more like the situation of accused Kos, who was a reserve policeman and to whom this circumstance did not aggravate his sentence. That's how the Defence understands the paragraph 732 of Kvocka judgement. So in conclusion, the Defence submits that in this case the Prosecution failed to establish beyond a reasonable doubt any of aggravating circumstances. Mitigating factors were discussed at length in our sentencing brief. On this occasion, we shall only emphasise the most important points with respect to evidence in this case. Pleading guilty before the commencement of trial is certainly an important mitigating factor in this case. Immediately after Darko Mrdja has been arrested, the Defence in this case tried to negotiate a plea bargain. Darko Mrdja himself was ready to do the same; however, the necessary conditions for that weren't met until later. The factual basis set forth in the initial indictment claimed that he was in command of the Intervention Squad that committed the massacre on Mount Vlasic on 21st August 1992. Besides that, indictment said that he ordered separations of civilians, their shooting, and that he said a sentence, "Here we shall make to exchange life for life and death. You know that." That's why the Defence also disagrees with today's arguments of learned colleague Tieger, because if we make a comparison between factual basis for the plea agreement and something which constitutes factual basis of the indictment, everybody can see major differences and why it was unacceptable for Darko Mrdja to accept his guilt under that indictment. Discovering the truth is -- this is a citation from the Erdemovic case. "Discovering the truth is a cornerstone of the rule of law and a fundamental step on the way to reconciliation: For it is the truth that cleanses the ethnic and the religious hatreds and begins the healing process. The International Tribunal must demonstrate that those who have the honesty to confess are treated fairly as part of process underpinned by principles of justice, fair trial, and protection of the fundamental rights of the individual." I want to take this opportunity to thank also to OTP and Mr. Tieger and Mr. Resch personally for their extraordinary efforts in reaching the truth in this case despite that from the aspect of proving its case the OTP did not have a difficult task and Defence had a very difficult one, because all potential witnesses regarding the real role of Darko Mrdja are themselves exposed to the criminal procedure. However, both parties in this case wanted to reach the truth as an ultimate goal of justice. In addition, a judgement based on a guilty plea before this Tribunal has far more significant effect in the country where I live, and that is Bosnia-Herzegovina, Republika Srpska. In this case, all complaints regarding the alleged partiality of this Tribunal are lost because Darko Mrdja is voluntarily admitting his guilt. The Defence has submitted personal circumstances as mitigating factors in this case. I want to take this opportunity to bring to the attention of this Honourable Trial Chamber the evidence that we have submitted. I only want to stress on this point that Darko Mrdja is known to be a man with a family, that he has two children, one of which is his son Nikola, who is ill. Before he was arrested, he worked very hard in order to preserve their existence. He had good relations with his neighbours, who are different ethnicities. If there had not been a war, Darko Mrdja would probably never have had a conflict with the law. Mrdja's family experiences great hardship due to his arrest. He is not in a position to help them economically but especially emotionally. The Defence want to emphasise again that Darko Mrdja has no prior convictions and there are no other procedures pending against him in any court, either before or after the events at Koricanske Stijene. We want to bring your attention to the statement of Ostoja Barasin, who was the chief of staff and then subsequently became the commander of the 5th Kozara Brigade, where Darko Mrdja served as a military policeman after the event on Koricanske Stijene and for the rest of the war. In this capacity, Darko Mrdja had significant authority in applying force and that he never misused his position. After the war, Darko Mrdja behaved in accordance with the law. From the time when he -- the crimes were committed until he was arrested, almost ten years passed. During that period, Darko Mrdja never broke the law. With such behaviour, Darko Mrdja continued after he was arrested, as can be seen from UN Detention Unit report. All of this tells us that the events at Koricanske Stijene represent one tragic episode, not a way of life, so from the point of view of rehabilitation -- from the point of view of rehabilitation, he deserves another chance in his life. Darko Mrdja today gave a statement from which we can see his sincere remorse for what he did. However, beside this statement, his behaviour after the crime was committed shows what his attitude regarding this crime. Immediately after, he expressed his desire to be designated to another military unit. I must -- I owe to you some explanation to that. In that time, there was not official requests for such transfer, so the Defence cannot to present you any evidence in that respect. But we have a document from which you can see that the transfer was -- had happened. And also his sister, Dragana Mrdja, gave a statement from which it can also be seen that he immediately, after Koricanske Stijene, was transferred and that he changed in some way his behaviour. We also, despite all criticism attached to expert witness Adolf Gallwitz but -- from various reason not connected with his -- with his authority and his skills and knowledge, I don't -- I think that we have to take a look on this report. And in that report it is said: "As a conclusion we have to state that at the time in question Darko Mrdja acted in a way of reduced self-control caused by acute stress or in a normal emotional reaction, with age, indoctrination, increased brutality, obedience, group-conforming conduct reducing the ability of independent thinking." Such conclusion must be considered in light of the behaviour of Darko Mrdja before this incident occurred. He and other members of the Intervention Squad escorted previously similar convoys of members of the non-Serb population to Doboj, but no casualties were reported. So in this case, he committed a crime when he implemented the orders given to him with fear to consequences that would have derived for any policeman who did not obey, especially given that the events occurred during the war. Those orders were undoubtedly illegal and Darko Mrdja knew the fact. However, in circumstances of this case, Darko Mrdja had a grounded reason to believe that he would be killed if he opposed such an order. Thus the Defence submits that in this case there existed duress as a mitigating factor in accordance with Article 7(4) of the Statute. Even if this Honourable Trial Chamber does not share this view, the Defence submits that those circumstances still need to be assessed along with the other individual circumstances, in accordance with Article 24(2) of the Statute. Regarding the age, it was already said. I will be very brief because, if I understand correctly, the OTP withdraw that it is a mitigating circumstance. We noticed that -- that in that paragraph was mixed two things, age of -- age of accused and age of victims -- age of victims, those two separate issues. We didn't say that Darko Mrdja's age is something what can be considered as independent mitigating circumstances. That doesn't mean that that circumstance also can be included in some personal circumstances of Mr. Darko Mrdja. So I will not talk about age of victims, but I don't think that is any more aggravating factor in -- from the submission of the Prosecutor. In addition to gravity of the crime and mitigating and aggravating factors, a Trial Chamber must also consider the purpose of punishment and the jurisprudence of the courts in the former Yugoslavia. The Defence submits that, in the interests of justice, the not-so-small jurisprudence of this Tribunal must be also considered. In relation to retribution as one of the goals of punishment, much has been said. The defence agrees that mere revenge cannot be considered as part of the purpose of punishment. That is a history of human civilisation. Evidence that supports this shows statistical data about the level of criminality in the countries where the death penalty exists compared with countries where the death penalty has been abolished. However, the Defence accepts that the punishment must fit the crime. As far as deterrence is concerned, we have to be cautious. There is no doubt that adequate punishment creates a consciousness in potential perpetrators that such behaviour is not allowed. However, a far more important factor in this respect is the level of detection and the per cent of punished perpetrators. That is a great difference when political leaders are concerned, especially those who led Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Common perpetrators of crimes form a much lower percentage of the accused persons charged before this Honourable Tribunal. However, we expect that in coming years this will change, if not in this Tribunal but in the Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina as well. But even if we have such a situation, it is realistic to expect that many of them who had similar or the same roles as Darko Mrdja and Drazen Erdemovic will not be punished. Such situations can send a wrong signal to all potential perpetrators of mass killings in future conflicts. They can easily learn that such behaviour is against the law but that there is high probability to remain unpunished with necessary measures of precaution. That is why the Defence considers that milder punishment can have deterrence effect in this case, because it will encourage much more people involved to admit their guilt. In that case, the percentage of those punished will be much higher. The Defence does not have exact data about the number of such people, but it considers that only in Srebrenica and in this case we deal with more than hundred of perpetrators. We already mentioned the sentencing practices in the courts of the former Yugoslavia. Even that practice does not bind this court. From the context of the previous paragraph we see that the vast majority of perpetrators who acted together with Darko Mrdja will have their proceedings before the newly established Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Defence consider that it will be unacceptable, due to the interests of justice, that persons who committed the same crime as perpetrators with all other similar cases be punished drastically different. It must be also considered that those persons will serve their sentence in Bosnia and Herzegovina. That is why the Defence consider that Darko Mrdja should not receive a sentence that cannot receive in domestic court. I must -- I must address here an issue that was raised by Mr. Tieger. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you one question in this respect. I followed your argument on the abolishment of capital punishment and what consequences it would have. What surprised me a bit is that you mentioned Article 1 of protocol 6. But Article 2, that specifically deals with capital punishment for crimes committed in time of war, is not addressed in whatever way. So this is not an issue that has been addressed by the Prosecution, but I would like to ask you to pay attention to the second article of protocol 6 as well, because that at least deals specifically with the issue that is crimes committed during time of war or in relation to a war.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I know that article. But that article, if I remember, or conventionally required to -- when establishing such crimes, you must put that it can be -- it can be done only in wartime. Articles what we have in -- regarding this particular criminal procedure we don't have wartime as -- as a factor. So I'm not sure that -- that capital punishment could be executed or judgement can be rendered with -- with capital punishment in this respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Didn't you quote Article 142 of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia Criminal Code in number 74 of your sentencing brief as the basis, the starting point for your reasoning, which reads: "Whoever, in violence of international law in time of war, armed conflict or occupation orders an attack against civilian population, tortures or inhumane treatment --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please read slowly. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I apologise. Which reads: "... shall be punished by no less than five years in prison or by the death penalty." Isn't that a -- an article of the Criminal Code which specifically refers to crimes committed in time of war?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. But you have to have a pronounced -- proclaimed time of war. We didn't have at that time in Bosnia-Herzegovina and Republika Srpska particularly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It says "in time of war --"

utterances.speaker: MR. DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "-- armed conflict or occupation." Doesn't that refer to an officially declared war, to an armed conflict not amounting to a declared war and, well, occupation of course a different category, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But as a prerequisite, Your Honour, you must have "or war" or something like that but proclaimed by the official body. There is jurisprudence I can provide you that those -- that article in -- is -- death penalty are concerned cannot be applied in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But why do you quote an article where you say now that it could not be applied, to give it as part of your argument? I mean, you are referring to this article, as I would understand, the article that would at time - not now any more, as you told us - would be the applicable law. And now you say but the requirements were not fulfilled. Was -- for normal murder, was the death -- was the capital punishment prescribed?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: No. For classic murder, no. It was from five to 15. But only for qualified forms of murder, that means murder two or more men -- people and other circumstances which are enumerated in Article 36, paragraph 2 of the Criminal Code.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But why did you quote Article 142 in order to give the basis for your argument that the abolishment -- the abolishing capital punishment would be the reason why it could be not any more than 15 years? I mean, why didn't you refer to other articles and say, "Well, Article 142 would not apply at all. Normal murder would be 10 years or 15 years or whatever." Why do you take 142 as a starting point of your argument if you tell us now that it would not have been applied -- applicable because the requirements were not met? I mean, what's the use then of quoting Article 142?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Obviously that -- we do not understand. This article is the legal frame for this crime of -- in the courts of Bosnia and Herzegovina. But I say -- what I say to you, that European Convention, which is directly applied in Bosnia-Herzegovina by the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina - and constitution is annex of Dayton Peace Agreement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: -- that abolished death penalty also in respect of this article, because prerequisites for this article to put the capital punishment you -- you don't have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I then ask you in this respect another question: In the text you provided to us, in the -- of the Dayton Agreement, it says, "The rights and freedoms set forth in the European Convention for the protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms shall apply directly in Bosnia and Herzegovina," referring to rights and freedoms. What is the right and the freedom granted to persons under the 6th protocol, Article 1?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: That death penalty is abolished, if I understand correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But that's not a right or a freedom of a person. I would say that the second part is that someone should not be -- should not be sentenced to death and a death penalty should not be executed. If, for example, I give you Belgian legislation, which still has the capital punishment but has another rule that says, "Well, of course we couldn't impose it and we can't enforce it." But you find in the Criminal Code of Belgium, which is part of the parties of the European Convention, you still find as punishment, capital punishment, but it's clear that this cannot be either imposed or improved and that's the language of the second line of Article 1 of protocol 6, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not -- I'm asking you what we are talking about, about enjoyment of rights and freedoms or duties upon states or protocol 6 is quite extraordinary in this respect. It doesn't even impose any duty on a state but declares that something is abolished, which of course creates the question: What exactly is abolished? The law which prescribes capital punishment or imposing capital punishment or enforcing capital punishment? It's a rather complicated matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Especially also in relation to Article 2 of protocol 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which I find only partly addressed in the sentencing brief. If you'd like to make any further comments on that, please do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: I will go on my last --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: -- part about sentencing practice of this Tribunal. Actually, we do not want to use this opportunity to make analyses in depth of previous Tribunal decisions. First of all, we do not want to provoke a polemic with our learned colleagues from the OTP. From the other side, we know that this Honourable Trial Chamber has far more knowledge about this issue than we have. We also acknowledge the fact that there are no two identical cases, but we wish to assist, we want to emphasise as a starting point the factors to be considered in order to find the most similar cases. First is gravity of crime; B, is similar factual basis (mass killing, one-day event, perpetrator executing orders, some level of duress); guilty plea before the commencement of the trial; remorse; level of cooperation with OTP; personal circumstances as (age, marital status, children, lack of criminal record, good behaviour in UN Detention Unit). Finally, we want to say that Darko Mrdja did commit the crime for which he is accused, but Darko Mrdja confesses his guilt. It is one day of his life. He expressed his remorse. He cooperated with OTP. He has family with ill baby. There is no other criminal procedure against him prior or before this tragic event. He is not criminal by his nature. In respect to all said above, the Defence respectfully suggests to this Honourable Trial Chamber that it would be just to impose a sentence in this case of not more than 15 years of imprisonment, including credit for time spent in the -- in the custody. Thank you for your attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Dimitrijevic. A few questions. First, Mr. Wachenheim, did you check the source of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. WACHENHEIM
utterances.text: Your Honour, I did, and I apologise for the work we created. It's been an apparent typing error. The right citation is volume 43, and then page 233, instead of 23. And then going on pages 234 and 235.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WACHENHEIM
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My next question would be Mr. Tieger has explained more or less what the decision is about. Do you agree with that or do you not agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WACHENHEIM
utterances.text: I do not agree with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then perhaps for sake of clarify, from the original source, I read - and I will try to translate what I find in the German language but -- into English - it says that: "Being a foreigner as such, taken as such, is not a reason to assume that there is a mitigating factor to be considered. It refers to Article 3 of the German constitution and says that this Article 3 would even a more favourable or more unfavourable position would even forbid to do that on the basis of where somewhere comes from. And then it says - and I'll later repeat it in German - it says: "Special circumstances can, however, in individual cases exceptionally justify a different judgement," or in German [German spoken]. Is this your understanding of what this case tells us? Although you did not agree with Mr. Tieger, but is this a fair representation of what the case is about? And then it continues to say that the lower court did not pay specific attention to issues raised in respect of specific -- special circumstances? Is that a correct understanding of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. WACHENHEIM
utterances.text: This is the correct understanding, Your Honour. And if I might just add, of course --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WACHENHEIM
utterances.text: -- we do have a lot of foreigners living in our country who might be socially integrated who might speak the language, and in those cases, of course, the mere fact that they are foreigners does not make any difference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WACHENHEIM
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand. Then, Mr. Tieger, would you be in any need to spend just a few lines on what I put to you earlier about the Krnojelac decision?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. With the miracle of modern technology, it's possible that I may be of assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Insofar as I can determine the jurisprudence on this issue begins with the Delalic case, which was cited by the Prosecution in its brief in Kunarac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And at paragraph 851 or 852 - I can't recall - the Kunarac -- and Kunarac is the case on which the Krnojelac Trial Chamber relied. So the Kunarac Trial Chamber goes back -- excuse me, the Krnojelac Trial Chamber goes back to the Kunarac case. And that reached -- which rejected the Prosecution argument regarding family members as saying that the Delalic case was "not wholly unambiguous," which seemed to have left the door open. And the Prosecution pursued that in the Krnojelac appeal. And in the -- in the Krnojelac appeal, the Appellate Chamber noted that, first, certain national jurisdictions have taken the impact on the family into consideration in imposing judgement. Second, the Appellate Chamber noted that even when specific family relations are not established by the evidence in the case explicitly, that the Trial Chamber should reasonably suppose that victims don't live in isolation but that they are related to other individuals. However, the trial -- the Appellate Chamber found the fact that the Trial Chamber didn't take that factor into account was not a sufficient reason to modify the sentence. Now, I -- and there's one more case that's worth noting, and that's Celebici, in which -- apparently at paragraph 1226 the Trial Chamber said that "The gravity of the offences of the kind charged have always been determined by the effect on the victim or at most on persons associated with the crime and nearest relations," which also seems to suggest the -- a possibility consistent with the Krnojelac Appeal Chamber.
